(p-١٥٦)﴿By the star when it sets﴾ ﴿your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾ ﴿nor does he speak from desire﴾ ﴿it is nothing but a revelation revealed﴾ ﴿taught to him by one mighty in power﴾ ﴿possessed of strength, and he stood firm﴾ ﴿while he was on the highest horizon﴾ ﴿then he drew near and came down﴾ ﴿and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾ ﴿so He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ ﴿the heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ ﴿will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ ﴿and he saw him in another descent﴾ ﴿at the Lote-tree of the utmost boundary﴾ [an-Najm: 14] ﴿near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾ [an-Najm: 15] ﴿when the Lote-tree was covered by that which covered it﴾ [an-Najm: 16] ﴿the gaze did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾ [an-Najm: 17] ﴿he certainly saw some of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ [an-Najm: 18] ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ [an-Najm: 19] ﴿and Manat, the third, the other one?﴾ [an-Najm: 20] ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ [an-Najm: 21] ﴿That, then, is an unjust division﴾ [an-Najm: 22] ﴿They are only names you have named, you and your forefathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority. They follow only conjecture and what their souls desire, though guidance has already come to them from their Lord﴾ [an-Najm: 23] ﴿Or does man have whatever he wishes?﴾ [an-Najm: 24] ﴿To Allah belongs the Hereafter and the first life﴾ [an-Najm: 25].

This surah is Meccan. Its connection to what precedes it is clear, since He said: ﴿Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"?﴾ [at-Tur: 33], meaning he invented the Qur'an. They attributed it to poetry and said: he is a soothsayer and a madman. So Allah swore that he (ﷺ) had not strayed, and that what he brings is a revelation from Allah. It is the first surah which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) proclaimed in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) while the polytheists were listening. In it he prostrated, and the believers, the polytheists, the jinn and mankind prostrated with him, except Abu Lahab, who raised a handful of dust to his forehead and said: "This is enough." The occasion of its revelation was the statement of the polytheists that Muhammad (ﷺ) fabricated the Qur'an.

Allah swore by "the star." Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Farra' and al-Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: it is the whole of the Qur'an when it was sent down, and it was sent down in portions over twenty years. al-Hasan and Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna said: here it is a noun of genus (ism jins), and the meaning is the stars when they set, i.e., when they go down. The poet said:

*So she spent the night counting the star in its place of hiding, swift to the hands of those who consume its embers.*

That is, she counts the stars. al-Hasan and Abu Hamza al-Thumali said: the stars when they fall scattered on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is that which pursues the devils, and this is supported by the language. al-Akhfash said: "the star when it rises," and its "falling" (hawiyyuhu) is its descent to the earth. Ibn Jubayr said: "the companion" is the Prophet (ﷺ), and his "falling" is his descent on the night of the Mi'raj (Ascension). It has been said: the star is a specific one. Mujahid and Sufyan said: it is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), and its "falling" is its setting at dawn. It is its name by predominance, and the Arabs do not say "the star" absolutely except for the Pleiades. From this is the saying of the Arabs:

*The star rose at night, so the shepherd sought a cloak.*

*The star rose in the morning, so the shepherd sought a blanket.*

It has been said: it is Sirius (ash-Shi'ra), and to it is the allusion in His saying: ﴿And that He is the Lord of Sirius﴾ [an-Najm: 49]. Soothsayers and astrologers speak about the unseen at its rising. It has been said: it is Venus (az-Zuhra), which was worshipped. It has been said: "the star" refers to the Companions. It has been said: it refers to the scholars, a singular noun used to indicate the plural. In the language, "hawa" means a tearing and its aim is the lowest, since its destination is there, even if it is not intended to go there. The poet said:

*The falling of the bucket, when the rope had let it go.*

From this is "hawa al-'uqab" (the eagle plunged).

﴿Your companion﴾: is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the address is to the Quraysh; that is, he is rightly guided and upright, and is not as you claim when you attribute to him error and deviation.

﴿Nor does he speak﴾: that is, the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, ﴿from desire﴾: that is, from the desire of his own soul and opinion.

﴿It is nothing but a revelation﴾ from Allah, (revealed) to him. It has been said: "nor does he speak" refers to the Qur'an, from desire and lust, as in His saying: ﴿This Our Book speaks against you with truth﴾ [al-Jathiya: 29]. "It is nothing but" refers to what he speaks. Or "it is nothing but" refers to the Qur'an.

(*'allamahu*): the pronoun refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), so the second object is omitted, meaning "taught him the revelation." Or it refers to the Qur'an, so the first object is omitted, meaning "taught him (the Messenger)." ﴿Mighty in power﴾ (shadid al-quwa): is Jibril (Gabriel), and this fits the attributes that follow, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Rabi'. al-Hasan said: ﴿mighty in power﴾ is Allah the Exalted, but this is far-fetched.

(*dhu mirra*): possessor of strength; from this is the saying: "Charity is not lawful for the wealthy, nor for one who possesses sound strength (*dhi mirra sawiyy*)." It has been said: possessor of a good form. It has been said: a tall and beautiful body. These two sayings fit only if "mighty in power" is Jibril (peace be upon him).

(*fastawa*): the pronoun refers to Allah according to al-Hasan's view, and likewise ﴿while he was on the highest horizon﴾ refers to Allah, in the sense of greatness, power and sovereignty. According to the view of the majority: (*fastawa*) means Jibril stood in the air, and ﴿he was on the highest horizon﴾: if the Messenger (ﷺ) saw him at Hira', having filled the horizon for him with six hundred wings. At that time he drew near to Muhammad until he was at a distance of two bow-lengths. Likewise he is the one seen in the second descent with six hundred wings at the Lote-tree, as said by al-Rabi' and al-Zajjaj. al-Tabari said, and al-Farra' (p-١٥٨) said: the meaning is that Jibril stood; and His saying "he" refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). In this interpretation there is coordination with the pronoun in the nominative without separation, which is the view of the Kufans. It may also be said: the pronoun in *istawa* refers to the Messenger, and "he" refers to Jibril, and "the highest" refers to the top of the head and what is near it. al-Hasan and Qatada said: it is the horizon of the rising of the sun.

al-Zamakhshari said: (*fastawa*) means he stood straight in his true form, not in the form in which he used to appear whenever he descended with revelation. He used to descend in the form of Dihya. That is because the Messenger (ﷺ) wished to see him in the form in which he was created, so he stood for him on the highest horizon, which is the horizon of the sun, and filled the horizon. It has been said: no prophet saw him in his true form except Muhammad (ﷺ), once on the earth and once in the heavens.

﴿Then he drew near﴾ to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿and came down﴾: that is, he hung over him in the air. The distance of his nearness to him was like ﴿two bow-lengths﴾, and these attributes were omitted, as Abu 'Ali said in his verse:

*And you have made me, of Khuzayma, a finger.*

That is, one having a distance of the measure of a finger. ﴿Or nearer﴾ according to your estimation, as in His saying: ﴿Or they are more﴾ [as-Saffat: 147].

﴿To His servant﴾: that is, to the servant of Allah, although no mention of His name, the Mighty and Majestic, has preceded, because it causes no confusion, as in His saying: ﴿He left none upon its back﴾ [Fatir: 45].

﴿What He revealed﴾: is an exaltation of the revelation that was revealed to him earlier. End of quotation. Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿Then he drew near﴾, the majority said: that is, Jibril drew near to Muhammad, upon both of them be prayers and peace, at Hira'. Ibn 'Abbas and Anas, in the hadith of the Night Journey (Isra'), said something that implies that the nearness is ascribed to Allah the Exalted. It has been said: the nearing was to Jibril. It has been said: to the Messenger (ﷺ), that is, his revelation, authority and power drew near. The correct view is that all that is in these verses is with Jibril, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾, for it implies a previous descent. As for what is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw his Lord before the night of the Isra', this is not correct. (*Dana*) is more general than (*tadalla*), so it clarifies the manner of the nearing: how it was, "two bow-lengths" in measure. Qatada and others said: its meaning is from one end of the bow to its other end. al-Hasan and Mujahid said: from the bowstring to the wood at the middle of the bow at the grip. Abu Razin said: it is not this bow, but the measure of two arms. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the bow here is a cubit by which lengths are measured. al-Tha'labi mentioned that it is from the dialect of the Hijaz.

(*fa-awha*): that is, Allah, ﴿to His servant﴾: that is, the Messenger (ﷺ), as said by Ibn 'Abbas. It has been said: ﴿to His servant﴾ refers to Jibril, and ﴿what He revealed﴾ is an ambiguity out of exaltation and magnification. What is known of it is the obligation of the prayers. al-Hasan said: Jibril revealed to the servant of Allah, Muhammad (ﷺ), what he revealed, like the first in its ambiguity. Ibn Zayd said: Jibril revealed to the servant of Allah, Muhammad (ﷺ), what Allah had revealed to Jibril (peace be upon him). al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿what He revealed﴾: He revealed to him that Paradise is forbidden to the prophets until you enter it, and forbidden to the nations until your nation enters it.

﴿The heart did not lie﴾: the heart (fu'ad) of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not lie about what he saw with his eyes of the form of Jibril; that is, his heart did not say, when he saw him, "I did not recognize you." The meaning is that he saw him with his eye and recognized him with his heart, and did not doubt that what he saw was true. End of quotation. The majority read *ma kadhaba* (lightened), meaning: the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not deny the thing that he saw; rather, it confirmed and verified it by seeing. (*kadhaba*) is transitive. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Salih said: Muhammad (ﷺ) saw Allah the Exalted with his heart. It has been said: what he saw with his eye, his heart did not deny; rather, it confirmed and verified it. It is possible that the implied meaning is "in what he saw."

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima and Ka'b al-Ahbar that Muhammad (ﷺ) saw his Lord with the eyes of his head. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, rejected this and said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about these verses, and he said to me: "It is Jibril, peace be upon him, in all of them." al-Hasan said: the meaning is what he saw of the things decreed by Allah the Exalted and His dominion. Abu Dharr asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "A light; how could I see Him?" Ka'b al-Ahbar said: Allah divided the seeing and speaking between Muhammad and Musa, peace be upon them both; Musa spoke twice, and Muhammad (ﷺ) saw twice. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: my hair stood up from hearing this, and she recited: ﴿Vision does not perceive Him, but He perceives vision﴾ [al-An'am: 103]. She, Ibn Mas'ud, Qatada and the majority went to the view that what was seen twice was Jibril: once on the earth, and once at the Lote-tree of the utmost boundary.

The majority read: ﴿Will you then dispute with him﴾: that is, will you argue with him about something he saw with his eyes and perceived? It is transitive with *'ala* because of the contention inherent in disputing. The verb "yara" is in the present form though the seeing has already occurred, indicating what may still occur later. ʿAlī, ʿAbdullāh, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Jahdari, Yaʿqub, Ibn Saʿdan, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read with a fatha on the *ta'* and sukun on the *mim*, the present of *maraytu*, meaning: you denied. It is said: "maraytuhu haqqahu" (I denied him his right) when you deny it. The poet said:

*If you mocked a brother of truth and nobility, you have indeed denied a brother who was never a denier.*

It is transitive with *'ala* in the sense of implication. When he (ﷺ) told the Quraysh about his matter in the Night Journey, they denied and mocked, until he described to them the House of al-Maqdis and the affair of their caravan and other things, which are detailed in the hadith of the Night Journey. ʿAbdullāh, as transmitted by Ibn Khalawayh, and al-Sha'bi, as mentioned by Shu'ba, read with a damma on the *ta'* and sukun on the *mim*, the present of *amraytu*. Abu Hatim said: this is an error.

﴿And he certainly saw him﴾: the object pronoun refers to Jibril (peace be upon him), as said by Ibn Mas'ud, 'A'isha, Mujahid and al-Rabi'.

﴿Another descent﴾ (*nazla ukhra*): that is, another time. That is, Jibril (peace be upon him) descended to him another time in his own form, and he saw him in it, and that was the night of the Mi'raj. "Ukhra" (another) implies a previous descent, which is what is understood from His saying: ﴿then he drew near﴾ — Jibril — ﴿and came down﴾: and that is descent and coming down from a height. Ibn 'Abbas and Ka'b al-Ahbar said: the pronoun refers to Allah, in accordance with their earlier statement that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw his Lord twice. "*Nazla*" is in the accusative: al-Zamakhshari said: the adverbial noun that is "marra" (a time) is in the accusative, because *fa'la* is a noun for the single instance of the verb. al-Hawfi and Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal).

She, Ibn Mas'ud, Qatada and the majority went to the view that what was seen twice was Jibril: once on the earth, and once at the Lote-tree of the utmost boundary.

The majority read: ﴿Will you then dispute with him﴾: that is, will you argue with him about something he saw with his eyes and perceived? The verb "yara" is in the present form though the seeing has already occurred, indicating what may still occur later. ʿAlī, ʿAbdullāh, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Jahdari, Yaʿqub, Ibn Saʿdan, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read with a fatha on the *ta'* and sukun on the *mim*, the present of *maraytu*, meaning: you denied. It is said: "maraytuhu haqqahu" (I denied him his right) when you deny it. The poet said:

*If you mocked a brother of truth and nobility, you have indeed denied a brother who was never a denier.*

It is transitive with *'ala* in the sense of implication. When he (ﷺ) told the Quraysh about his matter in the Night Journey, they denied and mocked, until he described to them the House of al-Maqdis and the affair of their caravan and other things, which are detailed in the hadith of the Night Journey. ʿAbdullāh, as transmitted by Ibn Khalawayh, and al-Sha'bi, as mentioned by Shu'ba, read with a damma on the *ta'* and sukun on the *mim*, the present of *amraytu*. ﴿Another descent﴾ (*nazla ukhra*): that is, another time. "Ukhra" (another) implies a previous descent, which is what is understood from His saying: ﴿then he drew near﴾ — Jibril — ﴿and came down﴾: and that is descent and coming down from a height. Ibn 'Abbas and Ka'b al-Ahbar said: the pronoun refers to Allah, in accordance with their earlier statement that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw his Lord twice. *The star rose in the morning, so the shepherd sought a blanket.*

(*dhu mirra*): possessor of strength; from this is the saying: "Charity is not lawful for the wealthy, nor for one who possesses sound strength (*dhi mirra sawiyy*)." It has been said: possessor of a good form. It has been said: a tall and beautiful body. These two sayings fit only if "mighty in power" is Jibril (peace be upon him).

(*fastawa*): the pronoun refers to Allah according to al-Hasan's view, and likewise ﴿while he was on the highest horizon﴾ refers to Allah, in the sense of greatness, power and sovereignty. According to the view of the majority: (*fastawa*) means Jibril stood in the air, and ﴿he was on the highest horizon﴾: if the Messenger (ﷺ) saw him at Hira', having filled the horizon for him with six hundred wings. At that time he drew near to Muhammad until he was at a distance of two bow-lengths. Likewise he is the one seen in the second descent with six hundred wings at the Lote-tree, as said by al-Rabi' and al-Zajjaj. al-Tabari said, and al-Farra' (p-١٥٨) said: the meaning is that Jibril stood; and His saying "he" refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). In this interpretation there is coordination with the pronoun in the nominative without separation, which is the view of the Kufans. It has been said: no prophet saw him in his true form except Muhammad (ﷺ), once on the earth and once in the heavens.

﴿Then he drew near﴾ to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿and came down﴾: that is, he hung over him in the air. The distance of his nearness to him was like ﴿two bow-lengths﴾, and these attributes were omitted, as Abu 'Ali said in his verse:

That is, one having a distance of the measure of a finger. ﴿Or nearer﴾ according to your estimation, as in His saying: ﴿Or they are more﴾ [as-Saffat: 147].

It has been said: to the Messenger (ﷺ), that is, his revelation, authority and power drew near. It is possible that the implied meaning is "in what he saw."

Likewise he is the one seen in the second descent with six hundred wings at the Lote-tree, as said by al-Rabi' and al-Zajjaj. al-Tabari said, and al-Farra' (p-١٥٨) said: the meaning is that Jibril stood; and His saying "he" refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). That is because the Messenger (ﷺ) wished to see him in the form in which he was created, so he stood for him on the highest horizon, which is the horizon of the sun, and filled the horizon. It has been said: no prophet saw him in his true form except Muhammad (ﷺ), once on the earth and once in the heavens.

﴿Then he drew near﴾ to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿and came down﴾: that is, he hung over him in the air. The distance of his nearness to him was like ﴿two bow-lengths﴾, and these attributes were omitted, as Abu 'Ali said in his verse:

*And you have made me, of Khuzayma, a finger.*

That is, one having a distance of the measure of a finger. ﴿Or nearer﴾ according to your estimation, as in His saying: ﴿Or they are more﴾ [as-Saffat: 147].

Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿Then he drew near﴾, the majority said: that is, Jibril drew near to Muhammad, upon both of them be prayers and peace, at Hira'. It has been said: to the Messenger (ﷺ), that is, his revelation, authority and power drew near. *The falling of the bucket, when the rope had let it go.*

From this is "hawa al-'uqab" (the eagle plunged).

Abu Raja', Abu Ja'far, Qatada, al-Jahdari, Khalid ibn Ilyas and Hisham from Ibn 'Amir read *ma kadhdhaba* (intensified). Ka'b al-Ahbar said: Allah divided the seeing and speaking between Muhammad and Musa, peace be upon them both; Musa spoke twice, and Muhammad (ﷺ) saw twice. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: my hair stood up from hearing this, and she recited: ﴿Vision does not perceive Him, but He perceives vision﴾ [al-An'am: 103]. She, Ibn Mas'ud, Qatada and the majority went to the view that what was seen twice was Jibril: once on the earth, and once at the Lote-tree of the utmost boundary.

The majority read: ﴿Will you then dispute with him﴾: that is, will you argue with him about something he saw with his eyes and perceived? It is transitive with *'ala* because of the contention inherent in disputing. The verb "yara" is in the present form though the seeing has already occurred, indicating what may still occur later. ʿAlī, ʿAbdullāh, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Jahdari, Yaʿqub, Ibn Saʿdan, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read with a fatha on the *ta'* and sukun on the *mim*, the present of *maraytu*, meaning: you denied. It is said: "maraytuhu haqqahu" (I denied him his right) when you deny it. The poet said:

*If you mocked a brother of truth and nobility, you have indeed denied a brother who was never a denier.*

It is transitive with *'ala* in the sense of implication. When he (ﷺ) told the Quraysh about his matter in the Night Journey, they denied and mocked, until he described to them the House of al-Maqdis and the affair of their caravan and other things, which are detailed in the hadith of the Night Journey. ʿAbdullāh, as transmitted by Ibn Khalawayh, and al-Sha'bi, as mentioned by Shu'ba, read with a damma on the *ta'* and sukun on the *mim*, the present of *amraytu*. Abu Hatim said: this is an error.

﴿And he certainly saw him﴾: the object pronoun refers to Jibril (peace be upon him), as said by Ibn Mas'ud, 'A'isha, Mujahid and al-Rabi'.

﴿Another descent﴾ (*nazla ukhra*): that is, another time. That is, Jibril (peace be upon him) descended to him another time in his own form, and he saw him in it, and that was the night of the Mi'raj. "Ukhra" (another) implies a previous descent, which is what is understood from His saying: ﴿then he drew near﴾ — Jibril — ﴿and came down﴾: and that is descent and coming down from a height. Ibn 'Abbas and Ka'b al-Ahbar said: the pronoun refers to Allah, in accordance with their earlier statement that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw his Lord twice. "*Nazla*" is in the accusative: al-Zamakhshari said: the adverbial noun that is "marra" (a time) is in the accusative, because *fa'la* is a noun for the single instance of the verb. al-Hawfi and Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal).

(p-١٥٦)﴿By the star when it sets﴾ ﴿your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾ ﴿nor does he speak from desire﴾ ﴿it is nothing but a revelation revealed﴾ ﴿taught to him by one mighty in power﴾ ﴿possessed of strength, and he stood firm﴾ ﴿while he was on the highest horizon﴾ ﴿then he drew near and came down﴾ ﴿and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾ ﴿so He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ ﴿the heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ ﴿will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ ﴿and he saw him in another descent﴾ ﴿at the Lote-tree of the utmost boundary﴾ [an-Najm: 14] ﴿near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾ [an-Najm: 15] ﴿when the Lote-tree was covered by that which covered it﴾ [an-Najm: 16] ﴿the gaze did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾ [an-Najm: 17] ﴿he certainly saw some of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ [an-Najm: 18] ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ [an-Najm: 19] ﴿and Manat, the third, the other one?﴾ [an-Najm: 20] ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ [an-Najm: 21] ﴿That, then, is an unjust division﴾ [an-Najm: 22] ﴿They are only names you have named, you and your forefathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority. They follow only conjecture and what their souls desire, though guidance has already come to them from their Lord﴾ [an-Najm: 23] ﴿Or does man have whatever he wishes?﴾ [an-Najm: 24] ﴿To Allah belongs the Hereafter and the first life﴾ [an-Najm: 25].

This surah is Meccan. Its connection to what precedes it is clear, since He said: ﴿Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"?﴾ [at-Tur: 33], meaning he invented the Qur'an. In it he prostrated, and the believers, the polytheists, the jinn and mankind prostrated with him, except Abu Lahab, who raised a handful of dust to his forehead and said: "This is enough." The poet said:

*So she spent the night counting the star in its place of hiding, swift to the hands of those who consume its embers.*

That is, she counts the stars. al-Hasan and Abu Hamza al-Thumali said: the stars when they fall scattered on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is that which pursues the devils, and this is supported by the language. al-Akhfash said: "the star when it rises," and its "falling" (hawiyyuhu) is its descent to the earth. Ibn Jubayr said: "the companion" is the Prophet (ﷺ), and his "falling" is his descent on the night of the Mi'raj (Ascension). It has been said: the star is a specific one. Mujahid and Sufyan said: it is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), and its "falling" is its setting at dawn. It is its name by predominance, and the Arabs do not say "the star" absolutely except for the Pleiades. From this is the saying of the Arabs:

*The star rose at night, so the shepherd sought a cloak.*

*The star rose in the morning, so the shepherd sought a blanket.*

It has been said: it is Sirius (ash-Shi'ra), and to it is the allusion in His saying: ﴿And that He is the Lord of Sirius﴾ [an-Najm: 49]. Soothsayers and astrologers speak about the unseen at its rising. It has been said: it is Venus (az-Zuhra), which was worshipped. It has been said: "the star" refers to the Companions. It has been said: it refers to the scholars, a singular noun used to indicate the plural. In the language, "hawa" means a tearing and its aim is the lowest, since its destination is there, even if it is not intended to go there. The poet said:

*The falling of the bucket, when the rope had let it go.*

From this is "hawa al-'uqab" (the eagle plunged).

﴿It is nothing but a revelation﴾ from Allah, (revealed) to him. It has been said: "nor does he speak" refers to the Qur'an, from desire and lust, as in His saying: ﴿This Our Book speaks against you with truth﴾ [al-Jathiya: 29]. "It is nothing but" refers to what he speaks. Or "it is nothing but" refers to the Qur'an.

(*dhu mirra*): possessor of strength; from this is the saying: "Charity is not lawful for the wealthy, nor for one who possesses sound strength (*dhi mirra sawiyy*)." It has been said: possessor of a good form. It has been said: a tall and beautiful body. These two sayings fit only if "mighty in power" is Jibril (peace be upon him).

(*fastawa*): the pronoun refers to Allah according to al-Hasan's view, and likewise ﴿while he was on the highest horizon﴾ refers to Allah, in the sense of greatness, power and sovereignty. According to the view of the majority: (*fastawa*) means Jibril stood in the air, and ﴿he was on the highest horizon﴾: if the Messenger (ﷺ) saw him at Hira', having filled the horizon for him with six hundred wings. At that time he drew near to Muhammad until he was at a distance of two bow-lengths. Likewise he is the one seen in the second descent with six hundred wings at the Lote-tree, as said by al-Rabi' and al-Zajjaj. al-Tabari said, and al-Farra' (p-١٥٨) said: the meaning is that Jibril stood; and His saying "he" refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). In this interpretation there is coordination with the pronoun in the nominative without separation, which is the view of the Kufans. It has been said: no prophet saw him in his true form except Muhammad (ﷺ), once on the earth and once in the heavens.

﴿Then he drew near﴾ to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿and came down﴾: that is, he hung over him in the air. The distance of his nearness to him was like ﴿two bow-lengths﴾, and these attributes were omitted, as Abu 'Ali said in his verse:

*And you have made me, of Khuzayma, a finger.*

That is, one having a distance of the measure of a finger. ﴿Or nearer﴾ according to your estimation, as in His saying: ﴿Or they are more﴾ [as-Saffat: 147].

﴿To His servant﴾: that is, to the servant of Allah, although no mention of His name, the Mighty and Majestic, has preceded, because it causes no confusion, as in His saying: ﴿He left none upon its back﴾ [Fatir: 45].

﴿What He revealed﴾: is an exaltation of the revelation that was revealed to him earlier. End of quotation. Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿Then he drew near﴾, the majority said: that is, Jibril drew near to Muhammad, upon both of them be prayers and peace, at Hira'. Ibn 'Abbas and Anas, in the hadith of the Night Journey (Isra'), said something that implies that the nearness is ascribed to Allah the Exalted. It has been said: the nearing was to Jibril. It has been said: to the Messenger (ﷺ), that is, his revelation, authority and power drew near. The correct view is that all that is in these verses is with Jibril, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾, for it implies a previous descent. As for what is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw his Lord before the night of the Isra', this is not correct. (*Dana*) is more general than (*tadalla*), so it clarifies the manner of the nearing: how it was, "two bow-lengths" in measure. Qatada and others said: its meaning is from one end of the bow to its other end. al-Hasan and Mujahid said: from the bowstring to the wood at the middle of the bow at the grip. Abu Razin said: it is not this bow, but the measure of two arms. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the bow here is a cubit by which lengths are measured. al-Tha'labi mentioned that it is from the dialect of the Hijaz.

(*fa-awha*): that is, Allah, ﴿to His servant﴾: that is, the Messenger (ﷺ), as said by Ibn 'Abbas. It has been said: ﴿to His servant﴾ refers to Jibril, and ﴿what He revealed﴾ is an ambiguity out of exaltation and magnification. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Salih said: Muhammad (ﷺ) saw Allah the Exalted with his heart. It has been said: what he saw with his eye, his heart did not deny; rather, it confirmed and verified it. It is possible that the implied meaning is "in what he saw."
