It is said: ḍūzā with a waw and with a hamza, and the hamza dialect was mentioned earlier in al-Mufradat as transmitted from al-Kisa'i. Al-Akhfash recited:

"If you turn away from her, she will demand from you, and if you are absent, your share is unjustly withheld and your nose is humbled."

﴿They are nothing but names you have named, you and your fathers, for which God has sent down no authority﴾: The explanation of its parallel was given in Surat Hud and in Surat al-A'raf. The majority read ﴿yattabi'ūn﴾ with the third-person ya'; 'Abdullah, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Waththab, Talhah, al-A'mash and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it with the second-person ta', (except the conjecture): which is the inclination of the soul toward one of two beliefs without proof. ﴿And what they desire﴾: that is, what they incline toward with pleasure. The soul always desires what is not the better, because it is naturally inclined to love pleasures, and only the intellect guides it to a good outcome.

﴿And there has certainly come to them from their Lord the guidance﴾: This is a rebuke to them, and what they are upon is falsehood; it is a parenthetical objection between the two clauses, meaning: they commit these ugly acts while guidance has already come to them, so they were the most deserving to accept it and abandon worshipping one whose worship benefits nothing.

﴿Or does man have whatever he wishes?﴾: This is connected to His saying: ﴿and what the souls desire﴾; rather, "man" here refers to the category, and ﴿whatever he wishes﴾ means whatever his wishes are set upon. That is, things and desires are not obtained by wishing; rather, the matter belongs to God. Your saying that your gods will intercede and bring you near in nearness is not something you have. It was said: their wish is their saying: "And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have the best with Him" [Fussilat: 50]. It was said: it is the statement of al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah: "I will surely be given wealth and children" [Maryam: 77]. It was said: some of them wished to be the Prophet.

﴿So to God belongs the Hereafter and the first﴾: meaning, He owns both, so He gives from them what He wills and withholds from whom He wills, and no one can attain anything from them except what God wills. He placed the Hereafter before the first because it is later in that respect, and because it is the rhyme-ending (fasilah), so he did not observe the existential order, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, to us belong the Hereafter and the first﴾ [al-Layl: 13].

Abu al-Baqa' said: it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning "another time" or "another vision."

﴿Near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾. It is said that it is a lote-tree in the seventh heaven. It is also said that it is in the sixth heaven, its fruit like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves like the ears of elephants. From its root flow the rivers that Allah the Exalted mentioned in His Book, and a rider would travel in its shade for seventy years without crossing it. Al-Muntaha (the Utmost Boundary) is the place of ending, because the knowledge of every knower ends at it, and none knows what lies beyond it except Allah the Exalted and Majestic; or because everyone who died in faith from every generation ends up there; or because what descends from the command of Allah the Exalted ends there, and neither the angels of the heights nor what ascends from the earth passes beyond it, nor do the angels of the lower realm pass beyond it; or because the spirits of the martyrs end there; or because it is as if it is at the far end and last part of Paradise; or because the angels and the prophets end there and stop at it; or because the knowledge of the prophets ends there and their knowledge falls short of what lies beyond it; or because deeds end there; or because of the ending of the one who is raised to it in honour. These are nine opinions.

﴿Near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾: that is, near the lote-tree. It is said that it may also mean "near the place of descent." Al-Hasan said: it is the Garden that Allah promised to the believers. Ibn ʿAbbas, in a report that differs from him, and Qatadah said: it is a garden to which the spirits of the martyrs resort, and it is not the one promised to the God-fearing, the Garden of Bliss. It is also said: it is the garden where the angels dwell. ʿAli, Abu al-Darda', Abu Hurayrah, Ibn al-Zubayr, Anas, Zirr, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Qatadah read: "jannahu" with a pronoun ending (the hā' of the Prophet, ﷺ), and "janna" as a past-tense verb, meaning: near it, the sheltering of Allah the Exalted and His fair handling covered him. It is also said that the meaning is: the night and the time of rest enveloped him. And it is said: He covered him with His shade and he entered into it. ʿĀʾishah and a group of Companions with her rejected this reading and said: "May Allah cover whoever reads it so." Since it is a reading that senior Companions of the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, recited, no one has the right to reject it. It is also said that ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, permitted it. The reading of the majority is: ﴿Garden of Refuge﴾, like His words in another verse: ﴿For them are gardens of refuge as a dwelling﴾ [al-Sajdah: 19].

﴿When there covers the lote-tree that which covers﴾: The vagueness of the relative pronoun and its clause here conveys magnification and amplification of the thing that covers it, for those are things whose description none knows except Allah the Exalted. It is also said: a vast multitude of angels covers it, worshipping Allah there. It is said: what covers it of the power of Allah the Exalted and the various attributes that He creates for it. Ibn Masʿud, Anas, Masruq, Mujahid and Ibrahim said: that is a locust of gold that covered it. Mujahid said: that is the change of its branches into pearls and rubies. It is related in a hadith: "I saw upon every leaf of its leaves an angel standing, glorifying Allah the Exalted." Also: a green silk canopy covers it; and also: colours cover it, which I do not know what they are. From Abu Hurayrah: the light of the Creator covers it. From al-Hasan: the light of the Lord of Might covered it and it shone. From Ibn ʿAbbas: the Lord of Might covered it, that is, His command, as came in Sahih Muslim in a marfuʿ report: "When there covered it of the command of Allah what covered." A parallel to this vagueness for the sake of magnification is: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 10], ﴿and the overturned cities He hurled down﴾ [al-Najm: 53], ﴿so there covered them what covered﴾ [al-Najm: 54].

﴿The eye did not swerve﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it did not incline this way or that. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, it fixed what it saw with a certain and correct fixing, without its gaze swerving or going beyond it, for he did not turn away from seeing the marvels which he was commanded to see and was enabled to see. ﴿Nor did it transgress﴾: nor did it go beyond what he was commanded to see. End of quote. Others said: ﴿nor did it transgress﴾: nor did it pass beyond the thing seen to something else, but it fell upon it with a correct falling, and this is an affirmation of the matter and a negation of doubt concerning it.

﴿Indeed he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾. It is said: al-Kubrā is the object of "saw," meaning he saw the greatest and mightiest signs, which are part of the signs of his Lord; that is, when he ascended to the heaven he saw the marvels of the dominion, and these are some of the signs of Allah. It is also said: "min āyāti" is in the position of the object, and al-Kubrā is an adjective of "āyāti rabbihi" (the signs of his Lord). A plural like this may be described with the description of the singular, and what makes it good here is that it forms the closing rhyme (fāṣilah), as in His words: ﴿that We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾ [Ṭāhā: 23], according to those who make it an adjective of "āyātinā" (Our signs). Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Masʿud said: that is, a green silk canopy that had filled the horizon. Ibn Zayd said: he saw Jibril in the form in which he is in the heaven.

"Have you then considered" (afa-ra'aytum): an address to the Quraysh. When he first established the message and followed it with mention of the greatness of Allah and His overwhelming power, with mention of tawhid and the prohibition of associating partners with Allah the Exalted, he made them consider the worthlessness of what they worshipped, which are the idols, and that they have no power. Al-Lat was an idol that the Arabs used to venerate. Qatadah said it was in al-Ta'if. Abu ʿUbaydah and others said it was in the Kaʿbah. Ibn Zayd said it was at Nakhlah near the market of ʿUkaz. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: Qatadah's view is more probable, and it is supported by the words of the poet:

"Thaqif fled to its Lat, in the manner of one who returns defeated and lost."

End of quote.

It is possible to reconcile these by saying that they were idols named after al-Lat, so each one reported the location of its idol. As for the tā' in al-Lāt, it is said to be original, the final radical of the word like the bā' in bāb, and its alif is apparently converted from a yā', because the root l-y-t exists. If a root l-w-t is found, it may be converted from a wāw. It is also said that the tā' is the feminine marker, and its pattern is fa'lah from lawā; it is said that they used to bend over it and devote themselves to worship there, or that they used to circle around it, and its final radical was dropped. The majority read "al-Lāt" with a light tā'; Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Mansur ibn al-Mu'tamir, Abu Salih, Talhah, Abu al-Jawza', Yaʿqub and Ibn Kathir in one transmission read it with a shadda. Ibn ʿAbbas said: this was a man in the market of ʿUkaz who would knead butter and parched flour beside a rock. It is said that this man was from Buhz, who kneaded parched flour for the pilgrims on a stone; when he died they worshipped the stone that had been beside him, out of reverence for that man, and named it after him. It is also said it was named after a man beside whom butter was kneaded with a ladle, and who fed the pilgrims. From Mujahid: a man used to knead parched flour in al-Ta'if, and they used to devote themselves at his grave, so they made him an idol. In al-Tahrir it is stated that it was an idol venerated by the Arabs. It is also said: al-Lat was a stone, and they named it after him. From Ibn Jubayr: a white rock that the Arabs used to worship and venerate. From Mujahid: small trees worshipped in their land, whose worship passed to the rock. End of the summary. The views concerning al-Lat are thus: was it an idol, or a stone on which something was kneaded, or a rock beside which something was kneaded, or the grave of al-Lat, or small trees and then a rock, or al-Lat itself. As for al-ʿUzzā, it is an idol. It is said: they named it after Ghatafan, and its root is the feminine of al-A'azz. "The Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to it, and he cut it down," and there came out of it a female devil, her hair loose, calling out woe, placing her hand on her head; so he struck her with the sword until he killed her, saying:

"O ʿUzza, your disbelief! No glorification for you! Indeed I have seen that Allah has humiliated you."

He returned and informed the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, who said, may the prayers and peace be upon him: "That was al-ʿUzzā, and she will never be worshipped again." Abu ʿUbaydah said: al-ʿUzzā and Manāt were at the Kaʿbah. End of quote. What supports this is the words of Abu Sufyan during some battles to the Muslims: "We have al-ʿUzzā, and you have no ʿUzzā." Ibn Zayd said: al-ʿUzzā was at al-Ta'if. Qatadah said: it was at Nakhlah. Reconciliation is possible, for in every place there was an idol named al-ʿUzzā, as we said about al-Lat, so each one reported about that named idol and its place.

﴿And Manāt﴾: It is said: a rock belonging to Hudhayl and Khuzaʿah. From Ibn ʿAbbas: it belonged to Thaqif. It is said: at al-Mushallal, a place of Qudayd between Makkah and Madinah; and it was the greatest of these idols in rank and the most numerous in worshippers, and the Aws and al-Khazraj used to raise the pilgrim's cry (ihlal) for it. This is considerable confusion about these idols and their locations, and what appears is that all three were in the Kaʿbah, because the addressees in "afa-ra'aytum" are the Quraysh. The majority read "Manāt" with a short vowel (maqsūr). It is said its pattern is fa'lah, and it was named Manāt because the blood of sacrifices used to be poured out (tumnā) beside it, that is, shed. Ibn Kathir read "Manā'ah" with a long vowel and a hamzah. It is said its pattern is maf'alah, so the alif is converted from a wāw, like maqālah, and the hamzah is an original radical derived from al-nawʾ (the rain-star), for they used to seek rain beside it by the stars, seeking blessing through it; but the shortened form is more famous. Jarir said:

"Does Zayd of Manāt threaten the might of Taym? Consider where your threat has led you astray."

Another said, with the long vowel and hamzah:

"Has not Taym, son of ʿAbd Manāʾah, reached us across the distance, the son of Tamim?"

"Al-Lāta, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt" are in the accusative by the verb "afa-ra'aytum," and it means "inform me." The second object of it is His words: ﴿Is for you the male and for Him the female?﴾, according to the rule established concerning the complement of "ara'ayta" when it means "inform me." No pronoun returns from the interrogative clause to al-Lat, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt, because His words "and for Him the female" have the sense of "and for Him these females," so this dispenses with the pronoun. They used to say of these idols that they were the daughters of Allah; so the meaning is: is for you the kind that is beloved and admired and present among you, and for Him the kind that is disparaged by your own claim, which is the burdensome one. The aptness of the expression "the female" lies in its being explicit about their belief that they are females and daughters of Allah the Exalted; and although the attachment of the feminine marker in al-Lāt and Manāt and the feminine alif in al-ʿUzzā suggests femininity, yet they named the masculine with a feminine form, so the word "al-Unthā" (the female) here is an explicit statement of their belief in their femininity. Its aptness is also that it comes as a closing rhyme; for if it had come as a pronoun, the structure would have been "Is for you the male and for Him they," which would not have formed a closing rhyme. Al-Zajjaj said: the way this verse is joined with what precedes it is that it says: tell me about your gods, do they have any of the power and greatness with which the Lord of Might was described in the previous verses? End of quote. He made the second object of "afa-ra'aytum" the interrogative clause he estimated, which was omitted because the preceding speech indicates it; and on his estimate, His words "Is for you the male and for Him the female" remain connected with what precedes it in meaning, not in grammatical construction, as we ourselves have said. I do not favour al-Zajjaj's phrase "the way this verse is joined with what precedes it"; had he said "the way this is connected" or "the way this is linked with what precedes it," it would have been better in terms of style, even though he meant the same thing.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "afa-ra'aytum" is an address to the Quraysh, and it is from sight with the eye, because he refers to visible bodies; had it been "ara'ayta" which is a request for a ruling, it would not have taken objects. End of quote. By "bodies" he means al-Lat, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt. "Ara'ayta" meaning a request for a ruling takes objects, as in: "Ara'ayta Zayd, what did he do?" His words "had it been ara'ayta which is a request for a ruling" refer to what grammarians say about it: that it means "inform me," which does not take objects; while "ara'ayta" meaning a request for a ruling takes two objects, one of which is in the accusative, and the other, usually, is an interrogative clause. This matter has been repeated for us before, and its beginning is in Surah al-An'am. Ibn ʿAtiyyah's speech shows that he had not studied what people have said about "ara'ayta" when it is a request for a ruling, according to his own terminology, which is the one meaning "inform me." The apparent meaning is that "al-thālithah al-ukhrā" (the third, the other) are two adjectives of Manāt, and they convey emphasis. It is said: since Manāt was the greatest of these idols, it was emphasised with these two descriptions, as you say: "I saw so-and-so and so-and-so," then you mention a third more exalted than them, saying: "and so-and-so, the other, who is of such standing." The word "ākhar" and "ukhrā" is used to describe the third of counted things, and this is explicit in the verse; from it is the words of Rabiʿah ibn Mukram:

"And indeed I made the two intercede with another, a third."

End of quote.

Ibn Abi Hatim... no, this is a translation task. Here is the translation.

Rabi'ah's view contradicts the verse, because a third idol came after another. And according to the view of this speaker that Manat is the greatest of these idols, the emphasis is due to her greatness. Do you not see His saying: "Then you mention a third, greater than the two"? Al-Zamakhshari said: "The other (al-ukhra) is a term of disparagement, referring to the one that comes last and is of low rank, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The last of them will say to the first of them﴾ [al-A'raf: 38], meaning: their followers say to their leaders and nobles. It is also possible that the 'first-ness' and precedence among them belongs to al-Lat and al-Uzza." End of quote.

The words "akhar" (another) and its feminine "ukhra" (other) were not established to express disparagement or praise. They only indicate the meaning of "other," except that it is a condition of both that they be of the same kind as what precedes them. If you say, "I passed by a man and another," it indicates only the meaning of "other," neither disparagement nor praise. Abu al-Baqa' said: "Al-ukhra is an emphasis, because the third can only be an 'other'." End of quote.

It was also said: al-ukhra is an attribute of al-Uzza, because she is the second of al-Lat, and the second is called "the other," and it was put last to match the rhyme endings of the verses. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: there is inversion in it; its sense is: "and al-Uzza, the other, and Manat, the third, the humiliated," because the first was an idol in the form of a human, al-Uzza was in the form of a plant, and Manat was in the form of a rock. A human is nobler than a plant, and a plant is nobler than an inanimate object. So the inanimate object comes last, and Manat is inanimate, so she is in the lowest of ranks. The reference of "those" (tilka) is to their division and their assessment that they have the males and God, exalted is He, has the females. They used to say: these idols and the angels are the daughters of God, exalted is He.

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: ﴿unjust﴾ means "unfair." Sufyan said: "deficient." Ibn Zayd said: "contrary." Mujahid and Muqatil said: "crooked." Al-Hasan said: "not balanced." Ibn Sirin said: "not even." All these statements are close in meaning.

The majority read ﴿ḍīzā﴾ without hamza, and the apparent view is that it is an attribute on the pattern fu'lā with a dammah on the fa', the kasrah being applied to make the ya' sound correct. It is also possible that it is a verbal noun on the pattern fi'lā, like dhikrā, and was described by it. Ibn Kathir read ḍi'zā with a hamza, which is directed as a verbal noun like dhikrā. Zayd ibn 'Ali read ḍīzā with a fatha on the ḍad and a sukun on the ya', which may be directed as a verbal noun like da'wā, described by it, or as an attribute like sakrā and nāqah kharamā. It is said: ḍūzā with a waw and with a hamza, and the hamza dialect was mentioned earlier in al-Mufradat as transmitted from al-Kisa'i. Al-Akhfash recited:

"If you turn away from her, she will demand from you, and if you are absent, your share is unjustly withheld and your nose is humbled."

﴿They are nothing but names you have named, you and your fathers, for which God has sent down no authority﴾: The explanation of its parallel was given in Surat Hud and in Surat al-A'raf. The majority read ﴿yattabi'ūn﴾ with the third-person ya'; 'Abdullah, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Waththab, Talhah, al-A'mash and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it with the second-person ta', (except the conjecture): which is the inclination of the soul toward one of two beliefs without proof. ﴿And what they desire﴾: that is, what they incline toward with pleasure. The soul always desires what is not the better, because it is naturally inclined to love pleasures, and only the intellect guides it to a good outcome.

﴿And there has certainly come to them from their Lord the guidance﴾: This is a rebuke to them, and what they are upon is falsehood; it is a parenthetical objection between the two clauses, meaning: they commit these ugly acts while guidance has already come to them, so they were the most deserving to accept it and abandon worshipping one whose worship benefits nothing.

﴿Or does man have whatever he wishes?﴾: This is connected to His saying: ﴿and what the souls desire﴾; rather, "man" here refers to the category, and ﴿whatever he wishes﴾ means whatever his wishes are set upon. That is, things and desires are not obtained by wishing; rather, the matter belongs to God. Your saying that your gods will intercede and bring you near in nearness is not something you have. It was said: their wish is their saying: "And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have the best with Him" [Fussilat: 50]. It was said: it is the statement of al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah: "I will surely be given wealth and children" [Maryam: 77]. It was said: some of them wished to be the Prophet.

﴿So to God belongs the Hereafter and the first﴾: meaning, He owns both, so He gives from them what He wills and withholds from whom He wills, and no one can attain anything from them except what God wills. He placed the Hereafter before the first because it is later in that respect, and because it is the rhyme-ending (fasilah), so he did not observe the existential order, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, to us belong the Hereafter and the first﴾ [al-Layl: 13].

Abu al-Baqa' said: it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning "another time" or "another vision."

﴿Near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾. It is said that it is a lote-tree in the seventh heaven. It is also said that it is in the sixth heaven, its fruit like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves like the ears of elephants. These are nine opinions.

﴿Near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾: that is, near the lote-tree. It is said that it may also mean "near the place of descent." Al-Hasan said: it is the Garden that Allah promised to the believers. Ibn ʿAbbas, in a report that differs from him, and Qatadah said: it is a garden to which the spirits of the martyrs resort, and it is not the one promised to the God-fearing, the Garden of Bliss. It is also said: it is the garden where the angels dwell. ʿAli, Abu al-Darda', Abu Hurayrah, Ibn al-Zubayr, Anas, Zirr, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Qatadah read: "jannahu" with a pronoun ending (the hā' of the Prophet, ﷺ), and "janna" as a past-tense verb, meaning: near it, the sheltering of Allah the Exalted and His fair handling covered him. It is also said that the meaning is: the night and the time of rest enveloped him. And it is said: He covered him with His shade and he entered into it. ʿĀʾishah and a group of Companions with her rejected this reading and said: "May Allah cover whoever reads it so." Since it is a reading that senior Companions of the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, recited, no one has the right to reject it. It is also said that ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, permitted it. The reading of the majority is: ﴿Garden of Refuge﴾, like His words in another verse: ﴿For them are gardens of refuge as a dwelling﴾ [al-Sajdah: 19].

﴿When there covers the lote-tree that which covers﴾: The vagueness of the relative pronoun and its clause here conveys magnification and amplification of the thing that covers it, for those are things whose description none knows except Allah the Exalted. It is also said: a vast multitude of angels covers it, worshipping Allah there. It is said: what covers it of the power of Allah the Exalted and the various attributes that He creates for it. Ibn Masʿud, Anas, Masruq, Mujahid and Ibrahim said: that is a locust of gold that covered it. Mujahid said: that is the change of its branches into pearls and rubies. It is related in a hadith: "I saw upon every leaf of its leaves an angel standing, glorifying Allah the Exalted." Also: a green silk canopy covers it; and also: colours cover it, which I do not know what they are. From Abu Hurayrah: the light of the Creator covers it. From al-Hasan: the light of the Lord of Might covered it and it shone. From Ibn ʿAbbas: the Lord of Might covered it, that is, His command, as came in Sahih Muslim in a marfuʿ report: "When there covered it of the command of Allah what covered." A parallel to this vagueness for the sake of magnification is: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 10], ﴿and the overturned cities He hurled down﴾ [al-Najm: 53], ﴿so there covered them what covered﴾ [al-Najm: 54].

﴿The eye did not swerve﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it did not incline this way or that. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, it fixed what it saw with a certain and correct fixing, without its gaze swerving or going beyond it, for he did not turn away from seeing the marvels which he was commanded to see and was enabled to see. ﴿Nor did it transgress﴾: nor did it go beyond what he was commanded to see. End of quote. Others said: ﴿nor did it transgress﴾: nor did it pass beyond the thing seen to something else, but it fell upon it with a correct falling, and this is an affirmation of the matter and a negation of doubt concerning it.

﴿Indeed he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾. It is said: al-Kubrā is the object of "saw," meaning he saw the greatest and mightiest signs, which are part of the signs of his Lord; that is, when he ascended to the heaven he saw the marvels of the dominion, and these are some of the signs of Allah. It is also said: "min āyāti" is in the position of the object, and al-Kubrā is an adjective of "āyāti rabbihi" (the signs of his Lord). A plural like this may be described with the description of the singular, and what makes it good here is that it forms the closing rhyme (fāṣilah), as in His words: ﴿that We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾ [Ṭāhā: 23], according to those who make it an adjective of "āyātinā" (Our signs). Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Masʿud said: that is, a green silk canopy that had filled the horizon. Ibn Zayd said: he saw Jibril in the form in which he is in the heaven.

"Have you then considered" (afa-ra'aytum): an address to the Quraysh. When he first established the message and followed it with mention of the greatness of Allah and His overwhelming power, with mention of tawhid and the prohibition of associating partners with Allah the Exalted, he made them consider the worthlessness of what they worshipped, which are the idols, and that they have no power. Al-Lat was an idol that the Arabs used to venerate. Qatadah said it was in al-Ta'if. Abu ʿUbaydah and others said it was in the Kaʿbah. Ibn Zayd said it was at Nakhlah near the market of ʿUkaz. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: Qatadah's view is more probable, and it is supported by the words of the poet:

"Thaqif fled to its Lat, in the manner of one who returns defeated and lost."

End of quote.

It is possible to reconcile these by saying that they were idols named after al-Lat, so each one reported the location of its idol. As for the tā' in al-Lāt, it is said to be original, the final radical of the word like the bā' in bāb, and its alif is apparently converted from a yā', because the root l-y-t exists. If a root l-w-t is found, it may be converted from a wāw. It is also said that the tā' is the feminine marker, and its pattern is fa'lah from lawā; it is said that they used to bend over it and devote themselves to worship there, or that they used to circle around it, and its final radical was dropped. The majority read "al-Lāt" with a light tā'; Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Mansur ibn al-Mu'tamir, Abu Salih, Talhah, Abu al-Jawza', Yaʿqub and Ibn Kathir in one transmission read it with a shadda. Ibn ʿAbbas said: this was a man in the market of ʿUkaz who would knead butter and parched flour beside a rock. It is said that this man was from Buhz, who kneaded parched flour for the pilgrims on a stone; when he died they worshipped the stone that had been beside him, out of reverence for that man, and named it after him. It is also said it was named after a man beside whom butter was kneaded with a ladle, and who fed the pilgrims. From Mujahid: a man used to knead parched flour in al-Ta'if, and they used to devote themselves at his grave, so they made him an idol. In al-Tahrir it is stated that it was an idol venerated by the Arabs. It is also said: al-Lat was a stone, and they named it after him. From Ibn Jubayr: a white rock that the Arabs used to worship and venerate. From Mujahid: small trees worshipped in their land, whose worship passed to the rock. End of the summary. The views concerning al-Lat are thus: was it an idol, or a stone on which something was kneaded, or a rock beside which something was kneaded, or the grave of al-Lat, or small trees and then a rock, or al-Lat itself. As for al-ʿUzzā, it is an idol. It is said: they named it after Ghatafan, and its root is the feminine of al-A'azz. "The Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to it, and he cut it down," and there came out of it a female devil, her hair loose, calling out woe, placing her hand on her head; so he struck her with the sword until he killed her, saying:

"O ʿUzza, your disbelief! No glorification for you! Indeed I have seen that Allah has humiliated you."

He returned and informed the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, who said, may the prayers and peace be upon him: "That was al-ʿUzzā, and she will never be worshipped again." Abu ʿUbaydah said: al-ʿUzzā and Manāt were at the Kaʿbah. End of quote. What supports this is the words of Abu Sufyan during some battles to the Muslims: "We have al-ʿUzzā, and you have no ʿUzzā." Ibn Zayd said: al-ʿUzzā was at al-Ta'if. Qatadah said: it was at Nakhlah. Reconciliation is possible, for in every place there was an idol named al-ʿUzzā, as we said about al-Lat, so each one reported about that named idol and its place.

﴿And Manāt﴾: It is said: a rock belonging to Hudhayl and Khuzaʿah. From Ibn ʿAbbas: it belonged to Thaqif. It is said: at al-Mushallal, a place of Qudayd between Makkah and Madinah; and it was the greatest of these idols in rank and the most numerous in worshippers, and the Aws and al-Khazraj used to raise the pilgrim's cry (ihlal) for it. This is considerable confusion about these idols and their locations, and what appears is that all three were in the Kaʿbah, because the addressees in "afa-ra'aytum" are the Quraysh. The majority read "Manāt" with a short vowel (maqsūr). It is said its pattern is fa'lah, and it was named Manāt because the blood of sacrifices used to be poured out (tumnā) beside it, that is, shed. Ibn Kathir read "Manā'ah" with a long vowel and a hamzah. It is said its pattern is maf'alah, so the alif is converted from a wāw, like maqālah, and the hamzah is an original radical derived from al-nawʾ (the rain-star), for they used to seek rain beside it by the stars, seeking blessing through it; but the shortened form is more famous. Jarir said:

"Does Zayd of Manāt threaten the might of Taym? Consider where your threat has led you astray."

Another said, with the long vowel and hamzah:

"Has not Taym, son of ʿAbd Manāʾah, reached us across the distance, the son of Tamim?"

"Al-Lāta, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt" are in the accusative by the verb "afa-ra'aytum," and it means "inform me." The second object of it is His words: ﴿Is for you the male and for Him the female?﴾, according to the rule established concerning the complement of "ara'ayta" when it means "inform me." No pronoun returns from the interrogative clause to al-Lat, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt, because His words "and for Him the female" have the sense of "and for Him these females," so this dispenses with the pronoun. They used to say of these idols that they were the daughters of Allah; so the meaning is: is for you the kind that is beloved and admired and present among you, and for Him the kind that is disparaged by your own claim, which is the burdensome one. The aptness of the expression "the female" lies in its being explicit about their belief that they are females and daughters of Allah the Exalted; and although the attachment of the feminine marker in al-Lāt and Manāt and the feminine alif in al-ʿUzzā suggests femininity, yet they named the masculine with a feminine form, so the word "al-Unthā" (the female) here is an explicit statement of their belief in their femininity. Its aptness is also that it comes as a closing rhyme; for if it had come as a pronoun, the structure would have been "Is for you the male and for Him they," which would not have formed a closing rhyme. Al-Zajjaj said: the way this verse is joined with what precedes it is that it says: tell me about your gods, do they have any of the power and greatness with which the Lord of Might was described in the previous verses? End of quote. He made the second object of "afa-ra'aytum" the interrogative clause he estimated, which was omitted because the preceding speech indicates it; and on his estimate, His words "Is for you the male and for Him the female" remain connected with what precedes it in meaning, not in grammatical construction, as we ourselves have said. I do not favour al-Zajjaj's phrase "the way this verse is joined with what precedes it"; had he said "the way this is connected" or "the way this is linked with what precedes it," it would have been better in terms of style, even though he meant the same thing.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "afa-ra'aytum" is an address to the Quraysh, and it is from sight with the eye, because he refers to visible bodies; had it been "ara'ayta" which is a request for a ruling, it would not have taken objects. End of quote. By "bodies" he means al-Lat, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt. "Ara'ayta" meaning a request for a ruling takes objects, as in: "Ara'ayta Zayd, what did he do?" His words "had it been ara'ayta which is a request for a ruling" refer to what grammarians say about it: that it means "inform me," which does not take objects; while "ara'ayta" meaning a request for a ruling takes two objects, one of which is in the accusative, and the other, usually, is an interrogative clause. This matter has been repeated for us before, and its beginning is in Surah al-An'am. Ibn ʿAtiyyah's speech shows that he had not studied what people have said about "ara'ayta" when it is a request for a ruling, according to his own terminology, which is the one meaning "inform me." The apparent meaning is that "al-thālithah al-ukhrā" (the third, the other) are two adjectives of Manāt, and they convey emphasis. It is said: since Manāt was the greatest of these idols, it was emphasised with these two descriptions, as you say: "I saw so-and-so and so-and-so," then you mention a third more exalted than them, saying: "and so-and-so, the other, who is of such standing." The word "ākhar" and "ukhrā" is used to describe the third of counted things, and this is explicit in the verse; from it is the words of Rabiʿah ibn Mukram:

"And indeed I made the two intercede with another, a third."

End of quote.

Ibn Abi Hatim... no, this is a translation task. Here is the translation.

Rabi'ah's view contradicts the verse, because a third idol came after another. And according to the view of this speaker that Manat is the greatest of these idols, the emphasis is due to her greatness. Do you not see His saying: "Then you mention a third, greater than the two"? Al-Zamakhshari said: "The other (al-ukhra) is a term of disparagement, referring to the one that comes last and is of low rank, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The last of them will say to the first of them﴾ [al-A'raf: 38], meaning: their followers say to their leaders and nobles. It is also possible that the 'first-ness' and precedence among them belongs to al-Lat and al-Uzza." End of quote.

The words "akhar" (another) and its feminine "ukhra" (other) were not established to express disparagement or praise. They only indicate the meaning of "other," except that it is a condition of both that they be of the same kind as what precedes them. If you say, "I passed by a man and another," it indicates only the meaning of "other," neither disparagement nor praise. Abu al-Baqa' said: "Al-ukhra is an emphasis, because the third can only be an 'other'." End of quote.

It was also said: al-ukhra is an attribute of al-Uzza, because she is the second of al-Lat, and the second is called "the other," and it was put last to match the rhyme endings of the verses. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: there is inversion in it; its sense is: "and al-Uzza, the other, and Manat, the third, the humiliated," because the first was an idol in the form of a human, al-Uzza was in the form of a plant, and Manat was in the form of a rock. A human is nobler than a plant, and a plant is nobler than an inanimate object. So the inanimate object comes last, and Manat is inanimate, so she is in the lowest of ranks. The reference of "those" (tilka) is to their division and their assessment that they have the males and God, exalted is He, has the females. They used to say: these idols and the angels are the daughters of God, exalted is He.

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: ﴿unjust﴾ means "unfair." Sufyan said: "deficient." Ibn Zayd said: "contrary." Mujahid and Muqatil said: "crooked." Al-Hasan said: "not balanced." Ibn Sirin said: "not even." All these statements are close in meaning.

The majority read ﴿ḍīzā﴾ without hamza, and the apparent view is that it is an attribute on the pattern fu'lā with a dammah on the fa', the kasrah being applied to make the ya' sound correct. It is also possible that it is a verbal noun on the pattern fi'lā, like dhikrā, and was described by it. Ibn Kathir read ḍi'zā with a hamza, which is directed as a verbal noun like dhikrā. Zayd ibn 'Ali read ḍīzā with a fatha on the ḍad and a sukun on the ya', which may be directed as a verbal noun like da'wā, described by it, or as an attribute like sakrā and nāqah kharamā. It is said: ḍūzā with a waw and with a hamza, and the hamza dialect was mentioned earlier in al-Mufradat as transmitted from al-Kisa'i. Al-Akhfash recited:

"If you turn away from her, she will demand from you, and if you are absent, your share is unjustly withheld and your nose is humbled."

﴿They are nothing but names you have named, you and your fathers, for which God has sent down no authority﴾: The explanation of its parallel was given in Surat Hud and in Surat al-A'raf. The majority read ﴿yattabi'ūn﴾ with the third-person ya'; 'Abdullah, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Waththab, Talhah, al-A'mash and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it with the second-person ta', (except the conjecture): which is the inclination of the soul toward one of two beliefs without proof. ﴿And what they desire﴾: that is, what they incline toward with pleasure. The soul always desires what is not the better, because it is naturally inclined to love pleasures, and only the intellect guides it to a good outcome.

﴿And there has certainly come to them from their Lord the guidance﴾: This is a rebuke to them, and what they are upon is falsehood; it is a parenthetical objection between the two clauses, meaning: they commit these ugly acts while guidance has already come to them, so they were the most deserving to accept it and abandon worshipping one whose worship benefits nothing.

﴿Or does man have whatever he wishes?﴾: This is connected to His saying: ﴿and what the souls desire﴾; rather, "man" here refers to the category, and ﴿whatever he wishes﴾ means whatever his wishes are set upon. That is, things and desires are not obtained by wishing; rather, the matter belongs to God. Your saying that your gods will intercede and bring you near in nearness is not something you have. It was said: their wish is their saying: "And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have the best with Him" [Fussilat: 50]. It was said: it is the statement of al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah: "I will surely be given wealth and children" [Maryam: 77]. It was said: some of them wished to be the Prophet.

﴿So to God belongs the Hereafter and the first﴾: meaning, He owns both, so He gives from them what He wills and withholds from whom He wills, and no one can attain anything from them except what God wills. He placed the Hereafter before the first because it is later in that respect, and because it is the rhyme-ending (fasilah), so he did not observe the existential order, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, to us belong the Hereafter and the first﴾ [al-Layl: 13].

Abu al-Baqa' said: it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning "another time" or "another vision."

﴿Near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾. It is said that it is a lote-tree in the seventh heaven. It is also said that it is in the sixth heaven, its fruit like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves like the ears of elephants. From its root flow the rivers that Allah the Exalted mentioned in His Book, and a rider would travel in its shade for seventy years without crossing it. Al-Muntaha (the Utmost Boundary) is the place of ending, because the knowledge of every knower ends at it, and none knows what lies beyond it except Allah the Exalted and Majestic; or because everyone who died in faith from every generation ends up there; or because what descends from the command of Allah the Exalted ends there, and neither the angels of the heights nor what ascends from the earth passes beyond it, nor do the angels of the lower realm pass beyond it; or because the spirits of the martyrs end there; or because it is as if it is at the far end and last part of Paradise; or because the angels and the prophets end there and stop at it; or because the knowledge of the prophets ends there and their knowledge falls short of what lies beyond it; or because deeds end there; or because of the ending of the one who is raised to it in honour. These are nine opinions.

﴿Near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾: that is, near the lote-tree. It is said that it may also mean "near the place of descent." Al-Hasan said: it is the Garden that Allah promised to the believers. Ibn ʿAbbas, in a report that differs from him, and Qatadah said: it is a garden to which the spirits of the martyrs resort, and it is not the one promised to the God-fearing, the Garden of Bliss. It is also said: it is the garden where the angels dwell. ʿAli, Abu al-Darda', Abu Hurayrah, Ibn al-Zubayr, Anas, Zirr, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Qatadah read: "jannahu" with a pronoun ending (the hā' of the Prophet, ﷺ), and "janna" as a past-tense verb, meaning: near it, the sheltering of Allah the Exalted and His fair handling covered him. It is also said that the meaning is: the night and the time of rest enveloped him. And it is said: He covered him with His shade and he entered into it. ʿĀʾishah and a group of Companions with her rejected this reading and said: "May Allah cover whoever reads it so." Since it is a reading that senior Companions of the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, recited, no one has the right to reject it. It is also said that ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, permitted it. The reading of the majority is: ﴿Garden of Refuge﴾, like His words in another verse: ﴿For them are gardens of refuge as a dwelling﴾ [al-Sajdah: 19].

﴿When there covers the lote-tree that which covers﴾: The vagueness of the relative pronoun and its clause here conveys magnification and amplification of the thing that covers it, for those are things whose description none knows except Allah the Exalted. It is also said: a vast multitude of angels covers it, worshipping Allah there. It is said: what covers it of the power of Allah the Exalted and the various attributes that He creates for it. Ibn Masʿud, Anas, Masruq, Mujahid and Ibrahim said: that is a locust of gold that covered it. Mujahid said: that is the change of its branches into pearls and rubies. It is related in a hadith: "I saw upon every leaf of its leaves an angel standing, glorifying Allah the Exalted." Also: a green silk canopy covers it; and also: colours cover it, which I do not know what they are. From Abu Hurayrah: the light of the Creator covers it. From al-Hasan: the light of the Lord of Might covered it and it shone. From Ibn ʿAbbas: the Lord of Might covered it, that is, His command, as came in Sahih Muslim in a marfuʿ report: "When there covered it of the command of Allah what covered." A parallel to this vagueness for the sake of magnification is: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 10], ﴿and the overturned cities He hurled down﴾ [al-Najm: 53], ﴿so there covered them what covered﴾ [al-Najm: 54].

﴿The eye did not swerve﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it did not incline this way or that. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, it fixed what it saw with a certain and correct fixing, without its gaze swerving or going beyond it, for he did not turn away from seeing the marvels which he was commanded to see and was enabled to see. ﴿Nor did it transgress﴾: nor did it go beyond what he was commanded to see. End of quote. Others said: ﴿nor did it transgress﴾: nor did it pass beyond the thing seen to something else, but it fell upon it with a correct falling, and this is an affirmation of the matter and a negation of doubt concerning it.

﴿Indeed he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾. It is said: al-Kubrā is the object of "saw," meaning he saw the greatest and mightiest signs, which are part of the signs of his Lord; that is, when he ascended to the heaven he saw the marvels of the dominion, and these are some of the signs of Allah. It is also said: "min āyāti" is in the position of the object, and al-Kubrā is an adjective of "āyāti rabbihi" (the signs of his Lord). A plural like this may be described with the description of the singular, and what makes it good here is that it forms the closing rhyme (fāṣilah), as in His words: ﴿that We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾ [Ṭāhā: 23], according to those who make it an adjective of "āyātinā" (Our signs). End of quote. By "bodies" he means al-Lat, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt. "Ara'ayta" meaning a request for a ruling takes objects, as in: "Ara'ayta Zayd, what did he do?" His words "had it been ara'ayta which is a request for a ruling" refer to what grammarians say about it: that it means "inform me," which does not take objects; while "ara'ayta" meaning a request for a ruling takes two objects, one of which is in the accusative, and the other, usually, is an interrogative clause. This matter has been repeated for us before, and its beginning is in Surah al-An'am. Ibn ʿAtiyyah's speech shows that he had not studied what people have said about "ara'ayta" when it is a request for a ruling, according to his own terminology, which is the one meaning "inform me." The apparent meaning is that "al-thālithah al-ukhrā" (the third, the other) are two adjectives of Manāt, and they convey emphasis. It is said: since Manāt was the greatest of these idols, it was emphasised with these two descriptions, as you say: "I saw so-and-so and so-and-so," then you mention a third more exalted than them, saying: "and so-and-so, the other, who is of such standing." The word "ākhar" and "ukhrā" is used to describe the third of counted things, and this is explicit in the verse; from it is the words of Rabiʿah ibn Mukram:

"And indeed I made the two intercede with another, a third."

End of quote.

Ibn Abi Hatim... no, this is a translation task. Here is the translation.

Rabi'ah's view contradicts the verse, because a third idol came after another. And according to the view of this speaker that Manat is the greatest of these idols, the emphasis is due to her greatness. Do you not see His saying: "Then you mention a third, greater than the two"? Al-Zamakhshari said: "The other (al-ukhra) is a term of disparagement, referring to the one that comes last and is of low rank, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The last of them will say to the first of them﴾ [al-A'raf: 38], meaning: their followers say to their leaders and nobles. It is also possible that the 'first-ness' and precedence among them belongs to al-Lat and al-Uzza." End of quote.

The words "akhar" (another) and its feminine "ukhra" (other) were not established to express disparagement or praise. They only indicate the meaning of "other," except that it is a condition of both that they be of the same kind as what precedes them. If you say, "I passed by a man and another," it indicates only the meaning of "other," neither disparagement nor praise. Abu al-Baqa' said: "Al-ukhra is an emphasis, because the third can only be an 'other'." End of quote.

It was also said: al-ukhra is an attribute of al-Uzza, because she is the second of al-Lat, and the second is called "the other," and it was put last to match the rhyme endings of the verses. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: there is inversion in it; its sense is: "and al-Uzza, the other, and Manat, the third, the humiliated," because the first was an idol in the form of a human, al-Uzza was in the form of a plant, and Manat was in the form of a rock. A human is nobler than a plant, and a plant is nobler than an inanimate object. So the inanimate object comes last, and Manat is inanimate, so she is in the lowest of ranks. The reference of "those" (tilka) is to their division and their assessment that they have the males and God, exalted is He, has the females. They used to say: these idols and the angels are the daughters of God, exalted is He.

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: ﴿unjust﴾ means "unfair." Sufyan said: "deficient." Ibn Zayd said: "contrary." Mujahid and Muqatil said: "crooked." Al-Hasan said: "not balanced." Ibn Sirin said: "not even." All these statements are close in meaning.

The majority read ﴿ḍīzā﴾ without hamza, and the apparent view is that it is an attribute on the pattern fu'lā with a dammah on the fa', the kasrah being applied to make the ya' sound correct. It is also possible that it is a verbal noun on the pattern fi'lā, like dhikrā, and was described by it. Ibn Kathir read ḍi'zā with a hamza, which is directed as a verbal noun like dhikrā. Zayd ibn 'Ali read ḍīzā with a fatha on the ḍad and a sukun on the ya', which may be directed as a verbal noun like da'wā, described by it, or as an attribute like sakrā and nāqah kharamā. It is said: ḍūzā with a waw and with a hamza, and the hamza dialect was mentioned earlier in al-Mufradat as transmitted from al-Kisa'i. Al-Akhfash recited:

"If you turn away from her, she will demand from you, and if you are absent, your share is unjustly withheld and your nose is humbled."

﴿They are nothing but names you have named, you and your fathers, for which God has sent down no authority﴾: The explanation of its parallel was given in Surat Hud and in Surat al-A'raf. The majority read ﴿yattabi'ūn﴾ with the third-person ya'; 'Abdullah, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Waththab, Talhah, al-A'mash and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it with the second-person ta', (except the conjecture): which is the inclination of the soul toward one of two beliefs without proof. ﴿And what they desire﴾: that is, what they incline toward with pleasure. The soul always desires what is not the better, because it is naturally inclined to love pleasures, and only the intellect guides it to a good outcome.

﴿And there has certainly come to them from their Lord the guidance﴾: This is a rebuke to them, and what they are upon is falsehood; it is a parenthetical objection between the two clauses, meaning: they commit these ugly acts while guidance has already come to them, so they were the most deserving to accept it and abandon worshipping one whose worship benefits nothing.

﴿Or does man have whatever he wishes?﴾: This is connected to His saying: ﴿and what the souls desire﴾; rather, "man" here refers to the category, and ﴿whatever he wishes﴾ means whatever his wishes are set upon. That is, things and desires are not obtained by wishing; rather, the matter belongs to God. Your saying that your gods will intercede and bring you near in nearness is not something you have. It was said: their wish is their saying: "And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have the best with Him" [Fussilat: 50]. It was said: it is the statement of al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah: "I will surely be given wealth and children" [Maryam: 77]. It was said: some of them wished to be the Prophet.

﴿So to God belongs the Hereafter and the first﴾: meaning, He owns both, so He gives from them what He wills and withholds from whom He wills, and no one can attain anything from them except what God wills. He placed the Hereafter before the first because it is later in that respect, and because it is the rhyme-ending (fasilah), so he did not observe the existential order, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, to us belong the Hereafter and the first﴾ [al-Layl: 13].

Abu al-Baqa' said: it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning "another time" or "another vision."

﴿Near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾. It is said that it is a lote-tree in the seventh heaven. It is also said that it is in the sixth heaven, its fruit like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves like the ears of elephants. From its root flow the rivers that Allah the Exalted mentioned in His Book, and a rider would travel in its shade for seventy years without crossing it. Al-Muntaha (the Utmost Boundary) is the place of ending, because the knowledge of every knower ends at it, and none knows what lies beyond it except Allah the Exalted and Majestic; or because everyone who died in faith from every generation ends up there; or because what descends from the command of Allah the Exalted ends there, and neither the angels of the heights nor what ascends from the earth passes beyond it, nor do the angels of the lower realm pass beyond it; or because the spirits of the martyrs end there; or because it is as if it is at the far end and last part of Paradise; or because the angels and the prophets end there and stop at it; or because the knowledge of the prophets ends there and their knowledge falls short of what lies beyond it; or because deeds end there; or because of the ending of the one who is raised to it in honour. These are nine opinions.

﴿Near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾: that is, near the lote-tree. It is said that it may also mean "near the place of descent." Al-Hasan said: it is the Garden that Allah promised to the believers. Ibn ʿAbbas, in a report that differs from him, and Qatadah said: it is a garden to which the spirits of the martyrs resort, and it is not the one promised to the God-fearing, the Garden of Bliss. It is also said: it is the garden where the angels dwell. ʿAli, Abu al-Darda', Abu Hurayrah, Ibn al-Zubayr, Anas, Zirr, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Qatadah read: "jannahu" with a pronoun ending (the hā' of the Prophet, ﷺ), and "janna" as a past-tense verb, meaning: near it, the sheltering of Allah the Exalted and His fair handling covered him. It is also said that the meaning is: the night and the time of rest enveloped him. And it is said: He covered him with His shade and he entered into it. ʿĀʾishah and a group of Companions with her rejected this reading and said: "May Allah cover whoever reads it so." Since it is a reading that senior Companions of the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, recited, no one has the right to reject it. It is also said that ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, permitted it. The reading of the majority is: ﴿Garden of Refuge﴾, like His words in another verse: ﴿For them are gardens of refuge as a dwelling﴾ [al-Sajdah: 19].

﴿When there covers the lote-tree that which covers﴾: The vagueness of the relative pronoun and its clause here conveys magnification and amplification of the thing that covers it, for those are things whose description none knows except Allah the Exalted. It is also said: a vast multitude of angels covers it, worshipping Allah there. It is said: what covers it of the power of Allah the Exalted and the various attributes that He creates for it. Ibn Masʿud, Anas, Masruq, Mujahid and Ibrahim said: that is a locust of gold that covered it. Mujahid said: that is the change of its branches into pearls and rubies. It is related in a hadith: "I saw upon every leaf of its leaves an angel standing, glorifying Allah the Exalted." Also: a green silk canopy covers it; and also: colours cover it, which I do not know what they are. From Abu Hurayrah: the light of the Creator covers it. From al-Hasan: the light of the Lord of Might covered it and it shone. From Ibn ʿAbbas: the Lord of Might covered it, that is, His command, as came in Sahih Muslim in a marfuʿ report: "When there covered it of the command of Allah what covered." A parallel to this vagueness for the sake of magnification is: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 10], ﴿and the overturned cities He hurled down﴾ [al-Najm: 53], ﴿so there covered them what covered﴾ [al-Najm: 54].

﴿The eye did not swerve﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it did not incline this way or that. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, it fixed what it saw with a certain and correct fixing, without its gaze swerving or going beyond it, for he did not turn away from seeing the marvels which he was commanded to see and was enabled to see. ﴿Nor did it transgress﴾: nor did it go beyond what he was commanded to see. End of quote. Others said: ﴿nor did it transgress﴾: nor did it pass beyond the thing seen to something else, but it fell upon it with a correct falling, and this is an affirmation of the matter and a negation of doubt concerning it.

﴿Indeed he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾. It is said: al-Kubrā is the object of "saw," meaning he saw the greatest and mightiest signs, which are part of the signs of his Lord; that is, when he ascended to the heaven he saw the marvels of the dominion, and these are some of the signs of Allah. It is also said: "min āyāti" is in the position of the object, and al-Kubrā is an adjective of "āyāti rabbihi" (the signs of his Lord). A plural like this may be described with the description of the singular, and what makes it good here is that it forms the closing rhyme (fāṣilah), as in His words: ﴿that We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾ [Ṭāhā: 23], according to those who make it an adjective of "āyātinā" (Our signs). Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Masʿud said: that is, a green silk canopy that had filled the horizon. Ibn Zayd said: he saw Jibril in the form in which he is in the heaven.

"Have you then considered" (afa-ra'aytum): an address to the Quraysh. When he first established the message and followed it with mention of the greatness of Allah and His overwhelming power, with mention of tawhid and the prohibition of associating partners with Allah the Exalted, he made them consider the worthlessness of what they worshipped, which are the idols, and that they have no power. Al-Lat was an idol that the Arabs used to venerate. Qatadah said it was in al-Ta'if. Abu ʿUbaydah and others said it was in the Kaʿbah. Ibn Zayd said it was at Nakhlah near the market of ʿUkaz. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: Qatadah's view is more probable, and it is supported by the words of the poet:

"Thaqif fled to its Lat, in the manner of one who returns defeated and lost."

End of quote.

It is possible to reconcile these by saying that they were idols named after al-Lat, so each one reported the location of its idol. As for the tā' in al-Lāt, it is said to be original, the final radical of the word like the bā' in bāb, and its alif is apparently converted from a yā', because the root l-y-t exists. If a root l-w-t is found, it may be converted from a wāw. It is also said that the tā' is the feminine marker, and its pattern is fa'lah from lawā; it is said that they used to bend over it and devote themselves to worship there, or that they used to circle around it, and its final radical was dropped. The majority read "al-Lāt" with a light tā'; Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Mansur ibn al-Mu'tamir, Abu Salih, Talhah, Abu al-Jawza', Yaʿqub and Ibn Kathir in one transmission read it with a shadda. Ibn ʿAbbas said: this was a man in the market of ʿUkaz who would knead butter and parched flour beside a rock. It is said that this man was from Buhz, who kneaded parched flour for the pilgrims on a stone; when he died they worshipped the stone that had been beside him, out of reverence for that man, and named it after him. It is also said it was named after a man beside whom butter was kneaded with a ladle, and who fed the pilgrims. From Mujahid: a man used to knead parched flour in al-Ta'if, and they used to devote themselves at his grave, so they made him an idol. In al-Tahrir it is stated that it was an idol venerated by the Arabs. It is also said: al-Lat was a stone, and they named it after him. From Ibn Jubayr: a white rock that the Arabs used to worship and venerate. From Mujahid: small trees worshipped in their land, whose worship passed to the rock. End of the summary. The views concerning al-Lat are thus: was it an idol, or a stone on which something was kneaded, or a rock beside which something was kneaded, or the grave of al-Lat, or small trees and then a rock, or al-Lat itself. As for al-ʿUzzā, it is an idol. It is said: they named it after Ghatafan, and its root is the feminine of al-A'azz. "The Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to it, and he cut it down," and there came out of it a female devil, her hair loose, calling out woe, placing her hand on her head; so he struck her with the sword until he killed her, saying:

"O ʿUzza, your disbelief! No glorification for you! Indeed I have seen that Allah has humiliated you."

He returned and informed the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, who said, may the prayers and peace be upon him: "That was al-ʿUzzā, and she will never be worshipped again." Abu ʿUbaydah said: al-ʿUzzā and Manāt were at the Kaʿbah. End of quote. What supports this is the words of Abu Sufyan during some battles to the Muslims: "We have al-ʿUzzā, and you have no ʿUzzā." Ibn Zayd said: al-ʿUzzā was at al-Ta'if. Qatadah said: it was at Nakhlah. Reconciliation is possible, for in every place there was an idol named al-ʿUzzā, as we said about al-Lat, so each one reported about that named idol and its place.

﴿And Manāt﴾: It is said: a rock belonging to Hudhayl and Khuzaʿah. From Ibn ʿAbbas: it belonged to Thaqif. It is said: at al-Mushallal, a place of Qudayd between Makkah and Madinah; and it was the greatest of these idols in rank and the most numerous in worshippers, and the Aws and al-Khazraj used to raise the pilgrim's cry (ihlal) for it. This is considerable confusion about these idols and their locations, and what appears is that all three were in the Kaʿbah, because the addressees in "afa-ra'aytum" are the Quraysh. The majority read "Manāt" with a short vowel (maqsūr). It is said its pattern is fa'lah, and it was named Manāt because the blood of sacrifices used to be poured out (tumnā) beside it, that is, shed. Ibn Kathir read "Manā'ah" with a long vowel and a hamzah. It is said its pattern is maf'alah, so the alif is converted from a wāw, like maqālah, and the hamzah is an original radical derived from al-nawʾ (the rain-star), for they used to seek rain beside it by the stars, seeking blessing through it; but the shortened form is more famous. Jarir said:

"Does Zayd of Manāt threaten the might of Taym? Consider where your threat has led you astray."

Another said, with the long vowel and hamzah:

"Has not Taym, son of ʿAbd Manāʾah, reached us across the distance, the son of Tamim?"

"Al-Lāta, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt" are in the accusative by the verb "afa-ra'aytum," and it means "inform me." The second object of it is His words: ﴿Is for you the male and for Him the female?﴾, according to the rule established concerning the complement of "ara'ayta" when it means "inform me." No pronoun returns from the interrogative clause to al-Lat, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt, because His words "and for Him the female" have the sense of "and for Him these females," so this dispenses with the pronoun. They used to say of these idols that they were the daughters of Allah; so the meaning is: is for you the kind that is beloved and admired and present among you, and for Him the kind that is disparaged by your own claim, which is the burdensome one. The aptness of the expression "the female" lies in its being explicit about their belief that they are females and daughters of Allah the Exalted; and although the attachment of the feminine marker in al-Lāt and Manāt and the feminine alif in al-ʿUzzā suggests femininity, yet they named the masculine with a feminine form, so the word "al-Unthā" (the female) here is an explicit statement of their belief in their femininity. Its aptness is also that it comes as a closing rhyme; for if it had come as a pronoun, the structure would have been "Is for you the male and for Him they," which would not have formed a closing rhyme. Al-Zajjaj said: the way this verse is joined with what precedes it is that it says: tell me about your gods, do they have any of the power and greatness with which the Lord of Might was described in the previous verses? End of quote. He made the second object of "afa-ra'aytum" the interrogative clause he estimated, which was omitted because the preceding speech indicates it; and on his estimate, His words "Is for you the male and for Him the female" remain connected with what precedes it in meaning, not in grammatical construction, as we ourselves have said. I do not favour al-Zajjaj's phrase "the way this verse is joined with what precedes it"; had he said "the way this is connected" or "the way this is linked with what precedes it," it would have been better in terms of style, even though he meant the same thing.
