The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "indahum" (they) refers to the people of Noah, and He made them ﴿more wrongdoing and more rebellious﴾, because they were in extreme defiance and harm toward Noah, peace be upon him, beating him until he could hardly move, and they were not affected by anything he called them to. Qatada said: He called them for a thousand years minus fifty years. Whenever one generation perished, another grew up, until a man would take his son by the hand and walk with him to Noah, warning him against him and saying: "O my son, my father walked with me to this man, and we were like you on that day, so beware lest you believe him." So the elder would die in disbelief, and the younger would grow up upon his father's testament. It is also said: the pronoun in "innahum" refers to those who preceded ʿAd, Thamud and the people of Noah, meaning they were more disbelieving than Quraysh and more rebellious, and in that is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The word hum may be an emphatic restatement of the object pronoun, or it may be a separator (fasl), since it occurs between a definite noun and an elative (af'al al-tafdil), and the second term of comparison after the predicate of kana was omitted, because it functions like the predicate of the subject, and omitting it is eloquent in that position, so likewise in the predicate of kana.

﴿And the overturned cities﴾: They are the cities of the people of Lot, by consensus of the exegetes. They were named so because they were overturned, and from this comes ifk (falsehood), because it is the reversal of truth into falsehood, afakahu fa-ʾtafaka (he turned it over, so it overturned). It is said: It may be intended by "the overturned" every place whose dwellings were overturned and whose locations were destroyed.

﴿Hawa (He hurled)﴾: That is, He caused them to sink into the earth after lifting them to the sky. Gabriel, peace be upon him, lifted them, then hurled them down to the earth. Al-Mubarrad said: He made it fall. Al-Hasan read: wa-l-mu'tafikat (plural). The apparent meaning is that ahwa governs al-mu'tafikah, and the verb was placed later because it serves as the closing rhyme (fasila). It is also possible that al-mu'tafikah is conjoined to what precedes it, and ahwa is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) clarifying the manner of their destruction, meaning: and the destruction of the overturned cities, while they were being hurled.

﴿Then there covered them what covered﴾: In this is an intensification of the punishment that befell them. When Gabriel, peace be upon him, overturned them, stones followed them and covered them. It is possible that fa"ala (the intensive form) here has the meaning of the simple form, so it is transitive to one object and the agent is ma, like His saying: ﴿Then there covered them of the sea what covered them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 78].

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?﴾: The ba' is for location (zarfiyya), and the address is to the listener. Tatamara means to be in doubt. It is a question with the meaning of denial: its favours, which are blessings, no listener could doubt them. Blessings and punishments were mentioned before, and all of them are called favours (ala'), because the punishments contain warning and admonition for those who take heed. Ya'qub and Ibn Muhaysin read: rabbika tamara, with a single, doubled ta'. Abu Malik al-Ghifari said: His saying "that no bearer of burden shall bear the burden of another" up to His saying "you dispute" is in the scrolls of Abraham and Moses, peace be upon them both.

﴿This is a warner﴾: Qatada, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Abu Ja'far said: The reference is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), with whom the beginning of the surah opened and with whom its end closes. It is also said: The reference is to the Qur'an. Abu Malik said: to what preceded of reports about the nations, meaning this is a warning among the warnings that came before. The word nadhir may be a verbal noun or an active participle, both derived from anadhara, and neither is regularly formed; rather the regular verbal noun is inthar, and the regular active participle is munthir. The plural nudhur is either a plural of the verbal noun or a plural of the active participle. If it is an active participle, describing the nudhur as "the first" is in the sense of a group. When He mentioned the destruction of those He had previously mentioned, and mentioned His saying "This is a warner," He stated that what he warned of is near in occurrence, so He said: ﴿The imminent one has drawn near﴾, meaning the one described as near in His saying: ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ [al-Qamar: 1], and it is the Resurrection.

﴿There is none to disclose it besides Allah﴾: That is, no soul will disclose its time and know it, as al-Tabari and al-Zajjaj said. Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: It is from removing harm and repelling it, meaning there is none to remove its calamity and terror. End of quote. The ha' in kashifa may be for intensification. Al-Rummani and a group said: It may be a verbal noun, like al-'aqibah and khaʾinat al-aʿyun (the treachery of the eyes), meaning there is no disclosing of it besides Allah. It is also said: it may be that the estimated sense is a state (hal) disclosing.

﴿Do you then wonder at this discourse﴾: That is, the Qur'an. ﴿And laugh, and do not weep﴾: Mocking, ﴿and do not weep﴾ out of fear of its threat.

﴿While you are sāmidūn (proud and heedless)﴾: Mujahid said: turning away. ʿIkrima said: heedless. Qatada said: unaware. Al-Suddi said: arrogant. Ibn ʿAbbas said: negligent. Al-Mubarrad said: stubbornly still. When they heard the Qur'an, they would sing to distract themselves from it. It is narrated that the Prophet, peace be upon him, was not seen laughing after its revelation.

﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship﴾: That is, pray to Him, and single Him out for worship, and do not worship al-Lat, al-ʿUzza, Manat, al-Shi'ra and other idols. Al-Baghawi related with a continuous chain of narration to ʿAbd Allah, who said: The first surah in which prostration was revealed was al-Najm. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prostrated, and those behind him prostrated, except for a man whom I saw take a handful of dirt and prostrate upon it. Then I saw him afterward, killed as a disbeliever, and the man was Umayya ibn Khalaf. It is also narrated that the polytheists prostrated with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). In the codex of Ubayy and ʿAbd Allah it reads: "you laugh" without the conjunction waw. Al-Hasan read: tu'jibuna, tudhikuna without the waw and with the ta' vowelled with damma, the jim and ha' with kasra. Regarding His saying: ﴿and do not weep﴾, there is an exhortation to weeping upon hearing the Qur'an. The prostration here is according to many people of knowledge, among them ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and authentic hadiths have come with it, though Malik does not consider it required here. From Zayd ibn Thabit: he recited it in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and did not prostrate. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 53, verses 33–62 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: (p-166) ﴿Have you considered the one who turned away,﴾ ﴿and gave a little and then held back?﴾ ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen so that he sees?﴾ ﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Musa,﴾ ﴿and Ibrahim, who fulfilled [his duty]?﴾ ﴿That no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another,﴾ ﴿and that man will have nothing but what he has striven for,﴾ ﴿and that his striving will be seen,﴾ ﴿then he will be recompensed with the fullest recompense,﴾ ﴿and that to your Lord is the final end,﴾ ﴿and that it is He who makes [people] laugh and weep,﴾ ﴿and that it is He who causes death and gives life,﴾ ﴿and that He created the two mates, male and female,﴾ ﴿from a drop of semen when it is emitted,﴾ ﴿and that upon Him is the second creation,﴾ ﴿and that it is He who enriches and suffices,﴾ ﴿and that He is the Lord of Sirius,﴾ ﴿and that He destroyed the first 'Ad,﴾ ﴿and Thamud, and spared none of them,﴾ ﴿and the people of Nuh before them, for they were more unjust and more rebellious,﴾ ﴿and the overturned [cities] He hurled down,﴾ ﴿and He covered them with what covered them,﴾ ﴿so which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?﴾ ﴿This is a warner of the same kind as the earlier warners,﴾ ﴿the impending [Hour] has drawn near,﴾ ﴿none besides Allah can reveal it,﴾ ﴿do you then marvel at this discourse,﴾ ﴿and laugh and not weep,﴾ ﴿while you are heedless?﴾ ﴿So prostrate yourselves to Allah and worship [Him].﴾

[The verse] "Have you considered" (ʾafaraʾayta): it is said that the verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. He had heard the recitation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), sat with him and was admonished by him, so he drew close to Islam, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) hoped for him. Then a man among the polytheists reproached him and said to him: "Will you abandon the religion of your fathers? Return to your religion and hold firmly to it, and I will bear for you everything you fear in the Hereafter, on condition that you give me such-and-such amount of wealth." Al-Walid agreed to this, turned back from what he had intended of Islam, went far astray, and gave part of that wealth to that man, then withheld the rest and became miserly. This was narrated by Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Muqatil. Al-Dahhak said: it is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who gave five camel-loads of wealth to a poor man among the Emigrants until he apostatised from his religion, and he guaranteed to bear his sins for his return [to unbelief]. Al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi, who would sometimes agree with the Prophet (ﷺ) on some matters. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: it concerns Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, who said: "By Allah, Muhammad only commands the noble qualities of character." It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi that it was revealed concerning ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan (may Allah be pleased with him); he used to give charity, and his milk-brother ʿAbd Allah ibn Saʿd ibn Abi Sarh said to him words similar to those of the speaker to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira with which we began. Al-Zamakhshari related the story in full and did not mention any other occasion of revelation (asbab al-nuzul) for it. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "All of that is, in my view, false, and ʿUthman (may Allah be pleased with him) is far above such a thing." End of quotation.

"Have you considered" (ʾafaraʾayta) here means "inform me." Its first object is the relative pronoun, and its second object is the interrogative clause, which is ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen﴾. "Turned away" (tawalla): i.e., he turned away from Islam. Al-Zamakhshari said: "(Turned away) means he abandoned his post on the day of Uhud." End of quotation. Since he took the verse to have been revealed concerning ʿUthman, he interpreted "turning away" in this way. When "turning away" is mentioned without a qualifier in the Qur'an, its most common usage is metaphorical for not entering into faith.

﴿and gave a little and then held back﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: he obeyed a little, then disobeyed. Mujahid said: he gave a little of himself by listening, then held back by ceasing. Al-Dahhak said: he gave a little of his wealth, then withheld. Muqatil said: he gave a little of good with his tongue, then cut off.

﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen﴾: i.e., does he know from the unseen that whoever bears the sins of another, the one whose burden is borne benefits from that? So is he, by virtue of this knowledge he has, seeing the truth and having insight into it? Or is he ignorant? Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿so that he sees﴾ means: he knows that what his brother said about bearing his burdens is true. It has been said: he knows his state in the Hereafter. Al-Zajjaj said: he sees the lifting of his sin in the Hereafter. It has also been said: he sees that what he heard of the Qur'an is false. Al-Kalbi said: a Qur'an was revealed to him, and he saw that what prevented him was true. It has been said: ﴿so that he sees﴾ means: he sees the parts [of the matter]. "Sees" (yaraa) may be understood in the sense of physical sight, i.e., he perceives what is hidden from others of what is unseen. It may also be understood in the sense of "knows," i.e., he knows the unseen just as he knows the seen.

﴿Or has he not been informed﴾: i.e., rather, has he not been told? ﴿of what is in the scriptures of Musa﴾, which is the Torah. ("And Ibrahim"): i.e., and in the scriptures of Ibrahim, which were revealed to him. These two prophets were singled out, may the best of blessings and peace be upon them. It has been said: this is because between Nuh and Ibrahim, people would hold a man accountable for his father, his son, his paternal uncle and his maternal uncle, a husband for his wife, and a slave for his master. The first to oppose them was Ibrahim. From the law of Ibrahim to the law of Musa, may peace be upon them both, people did not hold a man accountable for another's crime.

﴿who fulfilled [his duty]﴾: Al-Jumhur read wafFa with a doubled fa. Abu Umama al-Bahili, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Abu Malik al-Ghifari, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ and Zayd ibn ʿAli read it with a single fa. The object of wafFa is not mentioned, so that it encompasses everything that could be its object: such as conveying the message, bearing the burdens of prophethood, patience in the sacrifice of his son, patience in separation from Isma'il and his mother, patience in the fire of Namrud, and his hosting of guests and serving them himself. He used to walk one farsakh every day seeking a guest; if he found one, he honoured him, and otherwise he intended to fast. Al-Hasan said: Allah never commanded him with anything except that he fulfilled it. ʿAta ibn al-Sa'ib said: he covenanted not to ask any creature. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Rabiʿ said: he fulfilled the obedience to Allah in the command to sacrifice his son. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: he fulfilled [the duty of] conveying the message and striving for the sake of Allah. ʿIkrima said: in these ten verses [he fulfilled the duty of ]﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear﴾ and what follows it. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada also said: he fulfilled what was obligatory upon him of obedience in its proper manner, and the branches of faith and Islam were perfected for him, so Allah granted him freedom from the Fire. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: he fulfilled the laws of Islam, thirty portions: ten in Bara'a (﴿Those who repent…﴾ etc.), ten in Qad aflaha (the chapter 23), and ten in al-Ahzab (﴿Indeed the Muslim men…﴾). Abu Umama said, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): he fulfilled four prayers each day. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: he fulfilled the condition of what he claimed, because Allah the Exalted said to him, "Submit," and he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds," so Allah demanded the validity of his claim, and tested him with his wealth, his child and himself, and found him faithful. End of quotation. There are other opinions of the exegetes besides these. It is appropriate that these opinions be taken as examples of what he fulfilled, not as a definitive specification. And "that" (ʾallā) is the lightened form of the heavy one, and it stands either as a substitute for "what" in His saying ﴿with what is in the scriptures﴾, or in the nominative position, as if someone said: "what is in their scriptures?" and it was answered: ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾. The explanation of ﴿no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ has already been given.

﴿and that man will have nothing but what he has striven for﴾: The apparent meaning is that "man" includes both the believer and the unbeliever, and that the restriction is to striving, so he has no striving other than his own. ʿIkrima said: this ruling was for the people of Ibrahim and Musa; but as for this Ummah, it has the striving of others as well, as indicated by the hadith of Saʿd ibn ʿUbada: "Will it benefit my mother if I give charity on her behalf?" He said: "Yes." Al-Rabi said: "man" here means the disbeliever; but as for the believer, he has what he strove for and what others strove for on his behalf. The governor of Khurasan, ʿAbd Allah ibn Tahir, asked al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl about this verse together with His saying ﴿Allah multiplies [the reward] for whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261]. He said: "He has by justice only what he strove for, and by grace what Allah wills." So ʿAbd Allah kissed al-Husayn's head. As for what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is abrogated (mansukha, i.e., superseded by a later ruling), it is not sound, because it is a report that contains no obligation. The majority hold that it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated). Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "The correct view in my opinion regarding this verse is that the core of the meaning is the lam in His words ﴿for man﴾. When you establish what it is that a person may rightly say belongs to him, you will find it is only his striving. Whatever is added after that, such as mercy through intercession, the care of a righteous father or righteous son, the multiplication of good deeds, or Allah's deliberate bestowal of grace and mercy beyond all this, is not 'for man,' and he cannot rightly say 'this is mine' about it, except by a figurative extension and by attaching it to what is literally his." This verse was used as evidence by those who hold that no one acts on behalf of another after his death, whether with the body or with wealth; but some scholars distinguished between the body and wealth. End of quotation.

"Striving" (saʿy) means earning. "Will be seen" (yurā) is passive: i.e., he will see it present on the Day of Resurrection. The display of deeds is an honour for the doer of good and a rebuke to the wrongdoer. The pronoun in ﴿yujzāhu﴾ (he will be recompensed) refers to man, and the object pronoun refers to striving; "recompense" (al-jazāʾ) is a verbal noun. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the recompense, and then He explained it with His saying ﴿the fullest recompense﴾." If it is an explanation of the accusative verbal noun in yujzāhu, then on what is it in the accusative? And if it is an appositive, then it is of the type of substitution of a noun for a pronoun that the noun explains, a matter of disagreement, and the correct view is that it is not permitted. Al-Jumhur read ﴿and that to your Lord﴾ and what follows it from ﴿and that He﴾ with an opening hamza (anna), coordinated with what precedes it. Abu al-Sammal read them with a kasra throughout, and in His saying ﴿the fullest﴾. The threat is to the disbeliever and the promise to the believer. The "final end" (muntaha) of a thing is its ultimate point and what it reaches, i.e., the reckoning of your Lord and the gathering for its sake, as He said: ﴿and to Allah is the final return﴾, i.e., to His recompense and His reckoning, or to His reward of Paradise and His punishment of Hellfire. This explanation fits what precedes it in the verse. It is narrated from Ubayy, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and that to your Lord is the final end﴾: "Do not reflect upon the Lord." And Anas narrated from him (ﷺ): "When the Lord is mentioned, then desist."

﴿and that it is He who makes [people] laugh and weep﴾: The apparent meaning is the literal reality of laughing and weeping. Mujahid said: He made the people of Paradise laugh and the people of Hellfire weep. It has been said: laughter is a metaphor for joy, and weeping for sorrow. It has been said: He made the earth laugh with vegetation and the sky weep with rain. It has been said: He gives life through faith and causes weeping through disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿makes laugh and weeps﴾ means: He created the two faculties of laughing and weeping." End of quotation. In this there is a hint of Mu'tazilism (i'tizal, the Mu'tazili doctrine), since the actions of servants, such as laughing, weeping and others, are in their view created by the servant and not by Allah the Exalted; therefore he said: "He created the two faculties of laughing and weeping."

﴿and that He created the two mates﴾ who are paired, male and female, or other animals: ﴿from a drop of semen when it is emitted﴾: i.e., when it is poured forth, and this is the seminal fluid. It is said: "al-rajul amná and manná" (the man emitted semen). Al-Akhfash said: "when it is emitted" means: it is created and measured from the emission of the one who emits, i.e., the Measurer measured.

﴿and that upon Him is the second creation﴾: i.e., the re-creation of bodies, that is, the gathering after decay. The word "upon Him" (ʿalayhi) indicates necessity, because the existence of the thing is certain. Since the disbelievers deny this second creation, the emphasis was made by saying "upon Him," meaning its existence is inevitable, as if He, may He be exalted, made it obligatory upon Himself. The disagreement in the reading of "al-nashʾa" was mentioned in Surah al-ʿAnkabut. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He said ʿalayhi (upon Him) because it is obligatory upon Him by wisdom, so that He may recompense for good and evil." End of quotation. This is in the manner of Mu'tazilism.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 53, verses 33–62 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And that He is the One who enriches and provides (aqna)﴾: That is, He causes [people] to acquire property. It is said: qanaytu al-mal (I acquired the wealth), and aqnaytuhu iyyahu (I caused him to acquire it), meaning I caused him to acquire it. The object of aghna and aqna is not mentioned because the intent is to attribute these two actions to Allah, exalted is He. The exegetes (mufassirun) have discussed this and said there are twelve opinions, such as their saying: "He enriched Himself and made His creation poor in need of Him." Since none of these opinions has evidence to specify it, they should be taken as examples. The Sirius star (al-Shi'ra) that was worshipped is al-ʿUbur. Al-Suddi said: Himyar and Khuza'a used to worship it. Others said: The first to worship it was Abu Kabsha, one of the forefathers of the Prophet (ﷺ) on his mothers' side, and his name was ʿAbd al-Shi'ra. For this reason, the polytheists of Quraysh would call him (ﷺ) "the son of Abi Kabsha." From this is the saying of Abu Sufyan: "Indeed, the affair of the son of Abi Kabsha has become prominent." Among the Arabs there were those who revered it without worshipping it, believing in its influence on the world, and that it is one of the speaking stars. The astrologers claim this and speak of unseen matters at its rising. It crosses the sky lengthwise, while the stars cross it widthwise. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: It is Mirzam al-Jawza' (Orion's belt).

﴿And that He destroyed the first ʿAd﴾: The word huwa (He) came between "anna" (that) and its predicate, and this occurs in His saying: ﴿And that He is the One who makes laugh﴾, ﴿And that He is the One who causes death﴾, ﴿And that He is the One who enriches﴾, ﴿And that He is the Lord of Sirius﴾. As for the first three, since some people may claim this, like Nimrod's saying: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾ [al-Baqara: 258], emphasis was needed that this belongs to Allah alone and not to anyone else. He is the One who makes laugh and makes weep, He is the One who causes death and gives life, and He is the true enricher and provider. If anyone claims this, there is no reality to it. As for ﴿And that He is the Lord of Sirius﴾, since it was worshipped besides Allah, exalted is He, the text states that He, exalted is He, is its Lord and Originator. Since the creation of the pair, the other creation (al-insha' al-akhar), and the destruction of ʿAd and those mentioned, no one can claim these, so there was no need for emphasis or explicit statement that He, exalted is He, is the doer of these. The first ʿAd are the people of Hud, and the other ʿAd is Iram. It is said: The "first" refers to the ancients, because they were the first nation to be destroyed after the people of Noah, peace be upon him. It is said: The "first" refers to the eminent ones who preceded in the world; this was stated by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Zayd and the majority said: It is because they are at the beginning and ancient of time, so they are more appropriately described as "first" compared to later nations. Al-Tabari said: They were described as "the first" because the later ʿAd was a tribe that was in Mecca along with the Amalekites, and they were the Banu Luqaym ibn Hizal. Al-Mubarrad said: The later ʿAd is Thamud, and the evidence for this is the saying of Zuhayr:

*Like the red [she-camel] of ʿAd, then she is suckled and weaned*

Al-Zahrawi mentioned this. It is also said: the later ʿAd are the tyrants. It is also said: [they came] before the first, because they were before Thamud. It is also said: Thamud came before ʿAd. It is also said: the first ʿAd is ʿAd ibn Iram ibn ʿAws ibn Sam ibn Noah, and the second ʿAd are descendants of the first ʿAd.

The majority read ﴿ʿAdan al-ula﴾ with tanwin on ʿAdan and kasra on it, because it met a silent letter, with the lam of al-ula being silent, and with the hamza after the lam being realized (tahqiq). Some people read it the same way, except that they transferred the vowel of the hamza to the lam and dropped the hamza. Nafi' and Abu ʿAmr read with idgham (assimilation) of the tanwin into the lam to which the vowel of the dropped hamza has been transferred, and this reading ('Adin) is attributed to al-Mazini and al-Mubarrad. The Arabs, when beginning after the transfer, say: al-hummuru (the donkeys) as lu-hummuru. So this reading came in the form of lu-hummuru, and there is no fault in it. Qalun made a hamza of the ʿayn of al-ula instead of the silent waw. Since there was no barrier between the damma and the waw, he imagined that the damma was on the waw and so he made it a hamza, as the poet said:

*The fire-kindlers most beloved to me are Musa*

Likewise, some read: ʿalā suʾqihi (on its stalk), and this is a directive of anomaly (shadhdh). In the codex of Ubayy, it reads ʿAda without tanwin, making it the name of a tribe, so it is not declined (ghayr munsarif) because of femininity and being a proper name. The evidence for femininity is describing it as al-ula (the first). The majority read: wa-Thamuda (and Thamud) declined (munsarif). Al-Hasan, ʿAsim and ʿIsma read it as not declined (ghayr munsarif).

﴿So He left none﴾: The apparent meaning is that the object of abqa refers to both ʿAd and Thamud together, meaning He left none of them, that is, He seized them for their sins. It is also said: ﴿So He left none﴾ means He left none of them, not even a single eye that blinks. This was said by al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf when it was said to him that the Thaqif were descendants of Thamud. He said: Allah, exalted is He, said: "And Thamud, He left none," and these people say: a remnant of them remained. The apparent meaning is the first view, because a group of Thamud had believed in Salih, peace be upon him, so Allah did not destroy them along with those who disbelieved in him.

﴿And the people of Noah before﴾: That is, before ʿAd and Thamud. They were the first nation of people on earth to deny, and Noah, peace be upon him, was the first messenger. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "indahum" (they) refers to the people of Noah, and He made them ﴿more wrongdoing and more rebellious﴾, because they were in extreme defiance and harm toward Noah, peace be upon him, beating him until he could hardly move, and they were not affected by anything he called them to. Qatada said: He called them for a thousand years minus fifty years. Whenever one generation perished, another grew up, until a man would take his son by the hand and walk with him to Noah, warning him against him and saying: "O my son, my father walked with me to this man, and we were like you on that day, so beware lest you believe him." So the elder would die in disbelief, and the younger would grow up upon his father's testament. It is also said: the pronoun in "innahum" refers to those who preceded ʿAd, Thamud and the people of Noah, meaning they were more disbelieving than Quraysh and more rebellious, and in that is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The word hum may be an emphatic restatement of the object pronoun, or it may be a separator (fasl), since it occurs between a definite noun and an elative (af'al al-tafdil), and the second term of comparison after the predicate of kana was omitted, because it functions like the predicate of the subject, and omitting it is eloquent in that position, so likewise in the predicate of kana.

﴿And the overturned cities﴾: They are the cities of the people of Lot, by consensus of the exegetes. They were named so because they were overturned, and from this comes ifk (falsehood), because it is the reversal of truth into falsehood, afakahu fa-ʾtafaka (he turned it over, so it overturned). It is said: It may be intended by "the overturned" every place whose dwellings were overturned and whose locations were destroyed.

﴿Hawa (He hurled)﴾: That is, He caused them to sink into the earth after lifting them to the sky. Gabriel, peace be upon him, lifted them, then hurled them down to the earth. Al-Mubarrad said: He made it fall. Al-Hasan read: wa-l-mu'tafikat (plural). The apparent meaning is that ahwa governs al-mu'tafikah, and the verb was placed later because it serves as the closing rhyme (fasila). It is also possible that al-mu'tafikah is conjoined to what precedes it, and ahwa is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) clarifying the manner of their destruction, meaning: and the destruction of the overturned cities, while they were being hurled.

﴿Then there covered them what covered﴾: In this is an intensification of the punishment that befell them. When Gabriel, peace be upon him, overturned them, stones followed them and covered them. It is possible that fa"ala (the intensive form) here has the meaning of the simple form, so it is transitive to one object and the agent is ma, like His saying: ﴿Then there covered them of the sea what covered them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 78].

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?﴾: The ba' is for location (zarfiyya), and the address is to the listener. Tatamara means to be in doubt. It is a question with the meaning of denial: its favours, which are blessings, no listener could doubt them. Blessings and punishments were mentioned before, and all of them are called favours (ala'), because the punishments contain warning and admonition for those who take heed. Ya'qub and Ibn Muhaysin read: rabbika tamara, with a single, doubled ta'. Abu Malik al-Ghifari said: His saying "that no bearer of burden shall bear the burden of another" up to His saying "you dispute" is in the scrolls of Abraham and Moses, peace be upon them both.

﴿This is a warner﴾: Qatada, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Abu Ja'far said: The reference is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), with whom the beginning of the surah opened and with whom its end closes. It is also said: The reference is to the Qur'an. Abu Malik said: to what preceded of reports about the nations, meaning this is a warning among the warnings that came before. The word nadhir may be a verbal noun or an active participle, both derived from anadhara, and neither is regularly formed; rather the regular verbal noun is inthar, and the regular active participle is munthir. The plural nudhur is either a plural of the verbal noun or a plural of the active participle. If it is an active participle, describing the nudhur as "the first" is in the sense of a group. When He mentioned the destruction of those He had previously mentioned, and mentioned His saying "This is a warner," He stated that what he warned of is near in occurrence, so He said: ﴿The imminent one has drawn near﴾, meaning the one described as near in His saying: ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ [al-Qamar: 1], and it is the Resurrection.

﴿There is none to disclose it besides Allah﴾: That is, no soul will disclose its time and know it, as al-Tabari and al-Zajjaj said. Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: It is from removing harm and repelling it, meaning there is none to remove its calamity and terror. End of quote. The ha' in kashifa may be for intensification. Al-Rummani and a group said: It may be a verbal noun, like al-'aqibah and khaʾinat al-aʿyun (the treachery of the eyes), meaning there is no disclosing of it besides Allah. It is also said: it may be that the estimated sense is a state (hal) disclosing.

﴿Do you then wonder at this discourse﴾: That is, the Qur'an. ﴿And laugh, and do not weep﴾: Mocking, ﴿and do not weep﴾ out of fear of its threat.

﴿While you are sāmidūn (proud and heedless)﴾: Mujahid said: turning away. ʿIkrima said: heedless. Qatada said: unaware. Al-Suddi said: arrogant. Ibn ʿAbbas said: negligent. Al-Mubarrad said: stubbornly still. When they heard the Qur'an, they would sing to distract themselves from it. It is narrated that the Prophet, peace be upon him, was not seen laughing after its revelation.

﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship﴾: That is, pray to Him, and single Him out for worship, and do not worship al-Lat, al-ʿUzza, Manat, al-Shi'ra and other idols. Al-Baghawi related with a continuous chain of narration to ʿAbd Allah, who said: The first surah in which prostration was revealed was al-Najm. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prostrated, and those behind him prostrated, except for a man whom I saw take a handful of dirt and prostrate upon it. Then I saw him afterward, killed as a disbeliever, and the man was Umayya ibn Khalaf. It is also narrated that the polytheists prostrated with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). In the codex of Ubayy and ʿAbd Allah it reads: "you laugh" without the conjunction waw. Al-Hasan read: tu'jibuna, tudhikuna without the waw and with the ta' vowelled with damma, the jim and ha' with kasra. Regarding His saying: ﴿and do not weep﴾, there is an exhortation to weeping upon hearing the Qur'an. The prostration here is according to many people of knowledge, among them ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and authentic hadiths have come with it, though Malik does not consider it required here. From Zayd ibn Thabit: he recited it in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and did not prostrate. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 53, verses 33–62 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: (p-166) ﴿Have you considered the one who turned away,﴾ ﴿and gave a little and then held back?﴾ ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen so that he sees?﴾ ﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Musa,﴾ ﴿and Ibrahim, who fulfilled [his duty]?﴾ ﴿That no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another,﴾ ﴿and that man will have nothing but what he has striven for,﴾ ﴿and that his striving will be seen,﴾ ﴿then he will be recompensed with the fullest recompense,﴾ ﴿and that to your Lord is the final end,﴾ ﴿and that it is He who makes [people] laugh and weep,﴾ ﴿and that it is He who causes death and gives life,﴾ ﴿and that He created the two mates, male and female,﴾ ﴿from a drop of semen when it is emitted,﴾ ﴿and that upon Him is the second creation,﴾ ﴿and that it is He who enriches and suffices,﴾ ﴿and that He is the Lord of Sirius,﴾ ﴿and that He destroyed the first 'Ad,﴾ ﴿and Thamud, and spared none of them,﴾ ﴿and the people of Nuh before them, for they were more unjust and more rebellious,﴾ ﴿and the overturned [cities] He hurled down,﴾ ﴿and He covered them with what covered them,﴾ ﴿so which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?﴾ ﴿This is a warner of the same kind as the earlier warners,﴾ ﴿the impending [Hour] has drawn near,﴾ ﴿none besides Allah can reveal it,﴾ ﴿do you then marvel at this discourse,﴾ ﴿and laugh and not weep,﴾ ﴿while you are heedless?﴾ ﴿So prostrate yourselves to Allah and worship [Him].﴾

[The verse] "Have you considered" (ʾafaraʾayta): it is said that the verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. He had heard the recitation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), sat with him and was admonished by him, so he drew close to Islam, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) hoped for him. Then a man among the polytheists reproached him and said to him: "Will you abandon the religion of your fathers? Return to your religion and hold firmly to it, and I will bear for you everything you fear in the Hereafter, on condition that you give me such-and-such amount of wealth." Al-Walid agreed to this, turned back from what he had intended of Islam, went far astray, and gave part of that wealth to that man, then withheld the rest and became miserly. This was narrated by Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Muqatil. Al-Dahhak said: it is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who gave five camel-loads of wealth to a poor man among the Emigrants until he apostatised from his religion, and he guaranteed to bear his sins for his return [to unbelief]. Al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi, who would sometimes agree with the Prophet (ﷺ) on some matters. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: it concerns Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, who said: "By Allah, Muhammad only commands the noble qualities of character." It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi that it was revealed concerning ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan (may Allah be pleased with him); he used to give charity, and his milk-brother ʿAbd Allah ibn Saʿd ibn Abi Sarh said to him words similar to those of the speaker to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira with which we began. Al-Zamakhshari related the story in full and did not mention any other occasion of revelation (asbab al-nuzul) for it. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "All of that is, in my view, false, and ʿUthman (may Allah be pleased with him) is far above such a thing." End of quotation.

"Have you considered" (ʾafaraʾayta) here means "inform me." Its first object is the relative pronoun, and its second object is the interrogative clause, which is ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen﴾. "Turned away" (tawalla): i.e., he turned away from Islam. Al-Zamakhshari said: "(Turned away) means he abandoned his post on the day of Uhud." End of quotation. Since he took the verse to have been revealed concerning ʿUthman, he interpreted "turning away" in this way. When "turning away" is mentioned without a qualifier in the Qur'an, its most common usage is metaphorical for not entering into faith.

﴿and gave a little and then held back﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: he obeyed a little, then disobeyed. Mujahid said: he gave a little of himself by listening, then held back by ceasing. Al-Dahhak said: he gave a little of his wealth, then withheld. Muqatil said: he gave a little of good with his tongue, then cut off.

﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen﴾: i.e., does he know from the unseen that whoever bears the sins of another, the one whose burden is borne benefits from that? So is he, by virtue of this knowledge he has, seeing the truth and having insight into it? Or is he ignorant? Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿so that he sees﴾ means: he knows that what his brother said about bearing his burdens is true. It has been said: he knows his state in the Hereafter. Al-Zajjaj said: he sees the lifting of his sin in the Hereafter. It has also been said: he sees that what he heard of the Qur'an is false. Al-Kalbi said: a Qur'an was revealed to him, and he saw that what prevented him was true. It has been said: ﴿so that he sees﴾ means: he sees the parts [of the matter]. "Sees" (yaraa) may be understood in the sense of physical sight, i.e., he perceives what is hidden from others of what is unseen. It may also be understood in the sense of "knows," i.e., he knows the unseen just as he knows the seen.

﴿Or has he not been informed﴾: i.e., rather, has he not been told? ﴿of what is in the scriptures of Musa﴾, which is the Torah. ("And Ibrahim"): i.e., and in the scriptures of Ibrahim, which were revealed to him. These two prophets were singled out, may the best of blessings and peace be upon them. It has been said: this is because between Nuh and Ibrahim, people would hold a man accountable for his father, his son, his paternal uncle and his maternal uncle, a husband for his wife, and a slave for his master. The first to oppose them was Ibrahim. From the law of Ibrahim to the law of Musa, may peace be upon them both, people did not hold a man accountable for another's crime.

﴿who fulfilled [his duty]﴾: Al-Jumhur read wafFa with a doubled fa. Abu Umama al-Bahili, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Abu Malik al-Ghifari, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ and Zayd ibn ʿAli read it with a single fa. The object of wafFa is not mentioned, so that it encompasses everything that could be its object: such as conveying the message, bearing the burdens of prophethood, patience in the sacrifice of his son, patience in separation from Isma'il and his mother, patience in the fire of Namrud, and his hosting of guests and serving them himself. He used to walk one farsakh every day seeking a guest; if he found one, he honoured him, and otherwise he intended to fast. Al-Hasan said: Allah never commanded him with anything except that he fulfilled it. ʿAta ibn al-Sa'ib said: he covenanted not to ask any creature. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Rabiʿ said: he fulfilled the obedience to Allah in the command to sacrifice his son. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: he fulfilled [the duty of] conveying the message and striving for the sake of Allah. ʿIkrima said: in these ten verses [he fulfilled the duty of ]﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear﴾ and what follows it. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada also said: he fulfilled what was obligatory upon him of obedience in its proper manner, and the branches of faith and Islam were perfected for him, so Allah granted him freedom from the Fire. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: he fulfilled the laws of Islam, thirty portions: ten in Bara'a (﴿Those who repent…﴾ etc.), ten in Qad aflaha (the chapter 23), and ten in al-Ahzab (﴿Indeed the Muslim men…﴾). Abu Umama said, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): he fulfilled four prayers each day. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: he fulfilled the condition of what he claimed, because Allah the Exalted said to him, "Submit," and he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds," so Allah demanded the validity of his claim, and tested him with his wealth, his child and himself, and found him faithful. End of quotation. There are other opinions of the exegetes besides these. It is appropriate that these opinions be taken as examples of what he fulfilled, not as a definitive specification. And "that" (ʾallā) is the lightened form of the heavy one, and it stands either as a substitute for "what" in His saying ﴿with what is in the scriptures﴾, or in the nominative position, as if someone said: "what is in their scriptures?" and it was answered: ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾. The explanation of ﴿no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ has already been given.

﴿and that man will have nothing but what he has striven for﴾: The apparent meaning is that "man" includes both the believer and the unbeliever, and that the restriction is to striving, so he has no striving other than his own. ʿIkrima said: this ruling was for the people of Ibrahim and Musa; but as for this Ummah, it has the striving of others as well, as indicated by the hadith of Saʿd ibn ʿUbada: "Will it benefit my mother if I give charity on her behalf?" He said: "Yes." Al-Rabi said: "man" here means the disbeliever; but as for the believer, he has what he strove for and what others strove for on his behalf. The governor of Khurasan, ʿAbd Allah ibn Tahir, asked al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl about this verse together with His saying ﴿Allah multiplies [the reward] for whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261]. He said: "He has by justice only what he strove for, and by grace what Allah wills." So ʿAbd Allah kissed al-Husayn's head. As for what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is abrogated (mansukha, i.e., superseded by a later ruling), it is not sound, because it is a report that contains no obligation. The majority hold that it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated). Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "The correct view in my opinion regarding this verse is that the core of the meaning is the lam in His words ﴿for man﴾. When you establish what it is that a person may rightly say belongs to him, you will find it is only his striving. Whatever is added after that, such as mercy through intercession, the care of a righteous father or righteous son, the multiplication of good deeds, or Allah's deliberate bestowal of grace and mercy beyond all this, is not 'for man,' and he cannot rightly say 'this is mine' about it, except by a figurative extension and by attaching it to what is literally his." This verse was used as evidence by those who hold that no one acts on behalf of another after his death, whether with the body or with wealth; but some scholars distinguished between the body and wealth. End of quotation.

"Striving" (saʿy) means earning. "Will be seen" (yurā) is passive: i.e., he will see it present on the Day of Resurrection. The display of deeds is an honour for the doer of good and a rebuke to the wrongdoer. The pronoun in ﴿yujzāhu﴾ (he will be recompensed) refers to man, and the object pronoun refers to striving; "recompense" (al-jazāʾ) is a verbal noun. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the recompense, and then He explained it with His saying ﴿the fullest recompense﴾." If it is an explanation of the accusative verbal noun in yujzāhu, then on what is it in the accusative? And if it is an appositive, then it is of the type of substitution of a noun for a pronoun that the noun explains, a matter of disagreement, and the correct view is that it is not permitted. Al-Jumhur read ﴿and that to your Lord﴾ and what follows it from ﴿and that He﴾ with an opening hamza (anna), coordinated with what precedes it. Abu al-Sammal read them with a kasra throughout, and in His saying ﴿the fullest﴾. The threat is to the disbeliever and the promise to the believer. The "final end" (muntaha) of a thing is its ultimate point and what it reaches, i.e., the reckoning of your Lord and the gathering for its sake, as He said: ﴿and to Allah is the final return﴾, i.e., to His recompense and His reckoning, or to His reward of Paradise and His punishment of Hellfire. This explanation fits what precedes it in the verse. It is narrated from Ubayy, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and that to your Lord is the final end﴾: "Do not reflect upon the Lord." And Anas narrated from him (ﷺ): "When the Lord is mentioned, then desist."

﴿and that it is He who makes [people] laugh and weep﴾: The apparent meaning is the literal reality of laughing and weeping. Mujahid said: He made the people of Paradise laugh and the people of Hellfire weep. It has been said: laughter is a metaphor for joy, and weeping for sorrow. It has been said: He made the earth laugh with vegetation and the sky weep with rain. It has been said: He gives life through faith and causes weeping through disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿makes laugh and weeps﴾ means: He created the two faculties of laughing and weeping." End of quotation. In this there is a hint of Mu'tazilism (i'tizal, the Mu'tazili doctrine), since the actions of servants, such as laughing, weeping and others, are in their view created by the servant and not by Allah the Exalted; therefore he said: "He created the two faculties of laughing and weeping."

﴿and that He created the two mates﴾ who are paired, male and female, or other animals: ﴿from a drop of semen when it is emitted﴾: i.e., when it is poured forth, and this is the seminal fluid. It is said: "al-rajul amná and manná" (the man emitted semen). Al-Akhfash said: "when it is emitted" means: it is created and measured from the emission of the one who emits, i.e., the Measurer measured.

﴿and that upon Him is the second creation﴾: i.e., the re-creation of bodies, that is, the gathering after decay. The word "upon Him" (ʿalayhi) indicates necessity, because the existence of the thing is certain. Since the disbelievers deny this second creation, the emphasis was made by saying "upon Him," meaning its existence is inevitable, as if He, may He be exalted, made it obligatory upon Himself. The disagreement in the reading of "al-nashʾa" was mentioned in Surah al-ʿAnkabut. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He said ʿalayhi (upon Him) because it is obligatory upon Him by wisdom, so that He may recompense for good and evil." End of quotation. This is in the manner of Mu'tazilism.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 53, verses 33–62 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And that He is the One who enriches and provides (aqna)﴾: That is, He causes [people] to acquire property. It is said: qanaytu al-mal (I acquired the wealth), and aqnaytuhu iyyahu (I caused him to acquire it), meaning I caused him to acquire it. The object of aghna and aqna is not mentioned because the intent is to attribute these two actions to Allah, exalted is He. The exegetes (mufassirun) have discussed this and said there are twelve opinions, such as their saying: "He enriched Himself and made His creation poor in need of Him." Since none of these opinions has evidence to specify it, they should be taken as examples. The Sirius star (al-Shi'ra) that was worshipped is al-ʿUbur. Al-Suddi said: Himyar and Khuza'a used to worship it. Others said: The first to worship it was Abu Kabsha, one of the forefathers of the Prophet (ﷺ) on his mothers' side, and his name was ʿAbd al-Shi'ra. For this reason, the polytheists of Quraysh would call him (ﷺ) "the son of Abi Kabsha." From this is the saying of Abu Sufyan: "Indeed, the affair of the son of Abi Kabsha has become prominent." Among the Arabs there were those who revered it without worshipping it, believing in its influence on the world, and that it is one of the speaking stars. The astrologers claim this and speak of unseen matters at its rising. It crosses the sky lengthwise, while the stars cross it widthwise. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: It is Mirzam al-Jawza' (Orion's belt).

﴿And that He destroyed the first ʿAd﴾: The word huwa (He) came between "anna" (that) and its predicate, and this occurs in His saying: ﴿And that He is the One who makes laugh﴾, ﴿And that He is the One who causes death﴾, ﴿And that He is the One who enriches﴾, ﴿And that He is the Lord of Sirius﴾. As for the first three, since some people may claim this, like Nimrod's saying: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾ [al-Baqara: 258], emphasis was needed that this belongs to Allah alone and not to anyone else. He is the One who makes laugh and makes weep, He is the One who causes death and gives life, and He is the true enricher and provider. If anyone claims this, there is no reality to it. As for ﴿And that He is the Lord of Sirius﴾, since it was worshipped besides Allah, exalted is He, the text states that He, exalted is He, is its Lord and Originator. Since the creation of the pair, the other creation (al-insha' al-akhar), and the destruction of ʿAd and those mentioned, no one can claim these, so there was no need for emphasis or explicit statement that He, exalted is He, is the doer of these. The first ʿAd are the people of Hud, and the other ʿAd is Iram. It is said: The "first" refers to the ancients, because they were the first nation to be destroyed after the people of Noah, peace be upon him. It is said: The "first" refers to the eminent ones who preceded in the world; this was stated by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Zayd and the majority said: It is because they are at the beginning and ancient of time, so they are more appropriately described as "first" compared to later nations. Al-Tabari said: They were described as "the first" because the later ʿAd was a tribe that was in Mecca along with the Amalekites, and they were the Banu Luqaym ibn Hizal. Al-Mubarrad said: The later ʿAd is Thamud, and the evidence for this is the saying of Zuhayr:

*Like the red [she-camel] of ʿAd, then she is suckled and weaned*

Al-Zahrawi mentioned this. It is also said: the later ʿAd are the tyrants. It is also said: [they came] before the first, because they were before Thamud. It is also said: Thamud came before ʿAd. It is also said: the first ʿAd is ʿAd ibn Iram ibn ʿAws ibn Sam ibn Noah, and the second ʿAd are descendants of the first ʿAd.

The majority read ﴿ʿAdan al-ula﴾ with tanwin on ʿAdan and kasra on it, because it met a silent letter, with the lam of al-ula being silent, and with the hamza after the lam being realized (tahqiq). Some people read it the same way, except that they transferred the vowel of the hamza to the lam and dropped the hamza. Nafi' and Abu ʿAmr read with idgham (assimilation) of the tanwin into the lam to which the vowel of the dropped hamza has been transferred, and this reading ('Adin) is attributed to al-Mazini and al-Mubarrad. The Arabs, when beginning after the transfer, say: al-hummuru (the donkeys) as lu-hummuru. So this reading came in the form of lu-hummuru, and there is no fault in it. Qalun made a hamza of the ʿayn of al-ula instead of the silent waw. Since there was no barrier between the damma and the waw, he imagined that the damma was on the waw and so he made it a hamza, as the poet said:

*The fire-kindlers most beloved to me are Musa*

Likewise, some read: ʿalā suʾqihi (on its stalk), and this is a directive of anomaly (shadhdh). In the codex of Ubayy, it reads ʿAda without tanwin, making it the name of a tribe, so it is not declined (ghayr munsarif) because of femininity and being a proper name. The evidence for femininity is describing it as al-ula (the first). The majority read: wa-Thamuda (and Thamud) declined (munsarif). Al-Hasan, ʿAsim and ʿIsma read it as not declined (ghayr munsarif).

﴿So He left none﴾: The apparent meaning is that the object of abqa refers to both ʿAd and Thamud together, meaning He left none of them, that is, He seized them for their sins. It is also said: ﴿So He left none﴾ means He left none of them, not even a single eye that blinks. This was said by al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf when it was said to him that the Thaqif were descendants of Thamud. He said: Allah, exalted is He, said: "And Thamud, He left none," and these people say: a remnant of them remained. The apparent meaning is the first view, because a group of Thamud had believed in Salih, peace be upon him, so Allah did not destroy them along with those who disbelieved in him.

﴿And the people of Noah before﴾: That is, before ʿAd and Thamud. They were the first nation of people on earth to deny, and Noah, peace be upon him, was the first messenger. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "indahum" (they) refers to the people of Noah, and He made them ﴿more wrongdoing and more rebellious﴾, because they were in extreme defiance and harm toward Noah, peace be upon him, beating him until he could hardly move, and they were not affected by anything he called them to. Qatada said: He called them for a thousand years minus fifty years. Whenever one generation perished, another grew up, until a man would take his son by the hand and walk with him to Noah, warning him against him and saying: "O my son, my father walked with me to this man, and we were like you on that day, so beware lest you believe him." So the elder would die in disbelief, and the younger would grow up upon his father's testament. It is also said: the pronoun in "innahum" refers to those who preceded ʿAd, Thamud and the people of Noah, meaning they were more disbelieving than Quraysh and more rebellious, and in that is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The word hum may be an emphatic restatement of the object pronoun, or it may be a separator (fasl), since it occurs between a definite noun and an elative (af'al al-tafdil), and the second term of comparison after the predicate of kana was omitted, because it functions like the predicate of the subject, and omitting it is eloquent in that position, so likewise in the predicate of kana.

﴿And the overturned cities﴾: They are the cities of the people of Lot, by consensus of the exegetes. They were named so because they were overturned, and from this comes ifk (falsehood), because it is the reversal of truth into falsehood, afakahu fa-ʾtafaka (he turned it over, so it overturned). It is said: It may be intended by "the overturned" every place whose dwellings were overturned and whose locations were destroyed.

﴿Hawa (He hurled)﴾: That is, He caused them to sink into the earth after lifting them to the sky. Gabriel, peace be upon him, lifted them, then hurled them down to the earth. Al-Mubarrad said: He made it fall. Al-Hasan read: wa-l-mu'tafikat (plural). The apparent meaning is that ahwa governs al-mu'tafikah, and the verb was placed later because it serves as the closing rhyme (fasila). It is also possible that al-mu'tafikah is conjoined to what precedes it, and ahwa is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) clarifying the manner of their destruction, meaning: and the destruction of the overturned cities, while they were being hurled.

﴿Then there covered them what covered﴾: In this is an intensification of the punishment that befell them. When Gabriel, peace be upon him, overturned them, stones followed them and covered them. It is possible that fa"ala (the intensive form) here has the meaning of the simple form, so it is transitive to one object and the agent is ma, like His saying: ﴿Then there covered them of the sea what covered them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 78].

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?﴾: The ba' is for location (zarfiyya), and the address is to the listener. Tatamara means to be in doubt. It is a question with the meaning of denial: its favours, which are blessings, no listener could doubt them. Blessings and punishments were mentioned before, and all of them are called favours (ala'), because the punishments contain warning and admonition for those who take heed. Ya'qub and Ibn Muhaysin read: rabbika tamara, with a single, doubled ta'. Abu Malik al-Ghifari said: His saying "that no bearer of burden shall bear the burden of another" up to His saying "you dispute" is in the scrolls of Abraham and Moses, peace be upon them both.

﴿This is a warner﴾: Qatada, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Abu Ja'far said: The reference is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), with whom the beginning of the surah opened and with whom its end closes. It is also said: The reference is to the Qur'an. Abu Malik said: to what preceded of reports about the nations, meaning this is a warning among the warnings that came before. The word nadhir may be a verbal noun or an active participle, both derived from anadhara, and neither is regularly formed; rather the regular verbal noun is inthar, and the regular active participle is munthir. The plural nudhur is either a plural of the verbal noun or a plural of the active participle. If it is an active participle, describing the nudhur as "the first" is in the sense of a group. When He mentioned the destruction of those He had previously mentioned, and mentioned His saying "This is a warner," He stated that what he warned of is near in occurrence, so He said: ﴿The imminent one has drawn near﴾, meaning the one described as near in His saying: ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ [al-Qamar: 1], and it is the Resurrection.

﴿There is none to disclose it besides Allah﴾: That is, no soul will disclose its time and know it, as al-Tabari and al-Zajjaj said. Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: It is from removing harm and repelling it, meaning there is none to remove its calamity and terror. End of quote. The ha' in kashifa may be for intensification. Al-Rummani and a group said: It may be a verbal noun, like al-'aqibah and khaʾinat al-aʿyun (the treachery of the eyes), meaning there is no disclosing of it besides Allah. It is also said: it may be that the estimated sense is a state (hal) disclosing.

﴿Do you then wonder at this discourse﴾: That is, the Qur'an. ﴿And laugh, and do not weep﴾: Mocking, ﴿and do not weep﴾ out of fear of its threat.

﴿While you are sāmidūn (proud and heedless)﴾: Mujahid said: turning away. ʿIkrima said: heedless. Qatada said: unaware. Al-Suddi said: arrogant. Ibn ʿAbbas said: negligent. Al-Mubarrad said: stubbornly still. When they heard the Qur'an, they would sing to distract themselves from it. It is narrated that the Prophet, peace be upon him, was not seen laughing after its revelation.

﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship﴾: That is, pray to Him, and single Him out for worship, and do not worship al-Lat, al-ʿUzza, Manat, al-Shi'ra and other idols. Al-Baghawi related with a continuous chain of narration to ʿAbd Allah, who said: The first surah in which prostration was revealed was al-Najm. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prostrated, and those behind him prostrated, except for a man whom I saw take a handful of dirt and prostrate upon it. Then I saw him afterward, killed as a disbeliever, and the man was Umayya ibn Khalaf. It is also narrated that the polytheists prostrated with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). In the codex of Ubayy and ʿAbd Allah it reads: "you laugh" without the conjunction waw. Al-Hasan read: tu'jibuna, tudhikuna without the waw and with the ta' vowelled with damma, the jim and ha' with kasra. Regarding His saying: ﴿and do not weep﴾, there is an exhortation to weeping upon hearing the Qur'an. The prostration here is according to many people of knowledge, among them ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and authentic hadiths have come with it, though Malik does not consider it required here. From Zayd ibn Thabit: he recited it in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and did not prostrate. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 53, verses 33–62 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: (p-166) ﴿Have you considered the one who turned away,﴾ ﴿and gave a little and then held back?﴾ ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen so that he sees?﴾ ﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Musa,﴾ ﴿and Ibrahim, who fulfilled [his duty]?﴾ ﴿That no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another,﴾ ﴿and that man will have nothing but what he has striven for,﴾ ﴿and that his striving will be seen,﴾ ﴿then he will be recompensed with the fullest recompense,﴾ ﴿and that to your Lord is the final end,﴾ ﴿and that it is He who makes [people] laugh and weep,﴾ ﴿and that it is He who causes death and gives life,﴾ ﴿and that He created the two mates, male and female,﴾ ﴿from a drop of semen when it is emitted,﴾ ﴿and that upon Him is the second creation,﴾ ﴿and that it is He who enriches and suffices,﴾ ﴿and that He is the Lord of Sirius,﴾ ﴿and that He destroyed the first 'Ad,﴾ ﴿and Thamud, and spared none of them,﴾ ﴿and the people of Nuh before them, for they were more unjust and more rebellious,﴾ ﴿and the overturned [cities] He hurled down,﴾ ﴿and He covered them with what covered them,﴾ ﴿so which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?﴾ ﴿This is a warner of the same kind as the earlier warners,﴾ ﴿the impending [Hour] has drawn near,﴾ ﴿none besides Allah can reveal it,﴾ ﴿do you then marvel at this discourse,﴾ ﴿and laugh and not weep,﴾ ﴿while you are heedless?﴾ ﴿So prostrate yourselves to Allah and worship [Him].﴾

[The verse] "Have you considered" (ʾafaraʾayta): it is said that the verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. He had heard the recitation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), sat with him and was admonished by him, so he drew close to Islam, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) hoped for him. Then a man among the polytheists reproached him and said to him: "Will you abandon the religion of your fathers? Return to your religion and hold firmly to it, and I will bear for you everything you fear in the Hereafter, on condition that you give me such-and-such amount of wealth." Al-Walid agreed to this, turned back from what he had intended of Islam, went far astray, and gave part of that wealth to that man, then withheld the rest and became miserly. This was narrated by Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Muqatil. Al-Dahhak said: it is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who gave five camel-loads of wealth to a poor man among the Emigrants until he apostatised from his religion, and he guaranteed to bear his sins for his return [to unbelief]. Al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi, who would sometimes agree with the Prophet (ﷺ) on some matters. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: it concerns Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, who said: "By Allah, Muhammad only commands the noble qualities of character." It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi that it was revealed concerning ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan (may Allah be pleased with him); he used to give charity, and his milk-brother ʿAbd Allah ibn Saʿd ibn Abi Sarh said to him words similar to those of the speaker to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira with which we began. Al-Zamakhshari related the story in full and did not mention any other occasion of revelation (asbab al-nuzul) for it. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "All of that is, in my view, false, and ʿUthman (may Allah be pleased with him) is far above such a thing." End of quotation.

"Have you considered" (ʾafaraʾayta) here means "inform me." Its first object is the relative pronoun, and its second object is the interrogative clause, which is ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen﴾. "Turned away" (tawalla): i.e., he turned away from Islam. Al-Zamakhshari said: "(Turned away) means he abandoned his post on the day of Uhud." End of quotation. Since he took the verse to have been revealed concerning ʿUthman, he interpreted "turning away" in this way. When "turning away" is mentioned without a qualifier in the Qur'an, its most common usage is metaphorical for not entering into faith.

﴿and gave a little and then held back﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: he obeyed a little, then disobeyed. Mujahid said: he gave a little of himself by listening, then held back by ceasing. Al-Dahhak said: he gave a little of his wealth, then withheld. Muqatil said: he gave a little of good with his tongue, then cut off.

﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen﴾: i.e., does he know from the unseen that whoever bears the sins of another, the one whose burden is borne benefits from that? So is he, by virtue of this knowledge he has, seeing the truth and having insight into it? Or is he ignorant? Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿so that he sees﴾ means: he knows that what his brother said about bearing his burdens is true. It has been said: he knows his state in the Hereafter. Al-Zajjaj said: he sees the lifting of his sin in the Hereafter. It has also been said: he sees that what he heard of the Qur'an is false. Al-Kalbi said: a Qur'an was revealed to him, and he saw that what prevented him was true. It has been said: ﴿so that he sees﴾ means: he sees the parts [of the matter]. "Sees" (yaraa) may be understood in the sense of physical sight, i.e., he perceives what is hidden from others of what is unseen. It may also be understood in the sense of "knows," i.e., he knows the unseen just as he knows the seen.

﴿Or has he not been informed﴾: i.e., rather, has he not been told? ﴿of what is in the scriptures of Musa﴾, which is the Torah. ("And Ibrahim"): i.e., and in the scriptures of Ibrahim, which were revealed to him. These two prophets were singled out, may the best of blessings and peace be upon them. It has been said: this is because between Nuh and Ibrahim, people would hold a man accountable for his father, his son, his paternal uncle and his maternal uncle, a husband for his wife, and a slave for his master. The first to oppose them was Ibrahim. From the law of Ibrahim to the law of Musa, may peace be upon them both, people did not hold a man accountable for another's crime.

﴿who fulfilled [his duty]﴾: Al-Jumhur read wafFa with a doubled fa. Abu Umama al-Bahili, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Abu Malik al-Ghifari, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ and Zayd ibn ʿAli read it with a single fa. The object of wafFa is not mentioned, so that it encompasses everything that could be its object: such as conveying the message, bearing the burdens of prophethood, patience in the sacrifice of his son, patience in separation from Isma'il and his mother, patience in the fire of Namrud, and his hosting of guests and serving them himself. He used to walk one farsakh every day seeking a guest; if he found one, he honoured him, and otherwise he intended to fast. Al-Hasan said: Allah never commanded him with anything except that he fulfilled it. ʿAta ibn al-Sa'ib said: he covenanted not to ask any creature. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Rabiʿ said: he fulfilled the obedience to Allah in the command to sacrifice his son. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: he fulfilled [the duty of] conveying the message and striving for the sake of Allah. ʿIkrima said: in these ten verses [he fulfilled the duty of ]﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear﴾ and what follows it. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada also said: he fulfilled what was obligatory upon him of obedience in its proper manner, and the branches of faith and Islam were perfected for him, so Allah granted him freedom from the Fire. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: he fulfilled the laws of Islam, thirty portions: ten in Bara'a (﴿Those who repent…﴾ etc.), ten in Qad aflaha (the chapter 23), and ten in al-Ahzab (﴿Indeed the Muslim men…﴾). Abu Umama said, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): he fulfilled four prayers each day. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: he fulfilled the condition of what he claimed, because Allah the Exalted said to him, "Submit," and he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds," so Allah demanded the validity of his claim, and tested him with his wealth, his child and himself, and found him faithful. End of quotation. There are other opinions of the exegetes besides these. It is appropriate that these opinions be taken as examples of what he fulfilled, not as a definitive specification. And "that" (ʾallā) is the lightened form of the heavy one, and it stands either as a substitute for "what" in His saying ﴿with what is in the scriptures﴾, or in the nominative position, as if someone said: "what is in their scriptures?" and it was answered: ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾. The explanation of ﴿no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ has already been given.

﴿and that man will have nothing but what he has striven for﴾: The apparent meaning is that "man" includes both the believer and the unbeliever, and that the restriction is to striving, so he has no striving other than his own. ʿIkrima said: this ruling was for the people of Ibrahim and Musa; but as for this Ummah, it has the striving of others as well, as indicated by the hadith of Saʿd ibn ʿUbada: "Will it benefit my mother if I give charity on her behalf?" He said: "Yes." Al-Rabi said: "man" here means the disbeliever; but as for the believer, he has what he strove for and what others strove for on his behalf. The governor of Khurasan, ʿAbd Allah ibn Tahir, asked al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl about this verse together with His saying ﴿Allah multiplies [the reward] for whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261]. He said: "He has by justice only what he strove for, and by grace what Allah wills." So ʿAbd Allah kissed al-Husayn's head. As for what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is abrogated (mansukha, i.e., superseded by a later ruling), it is not sound, because it is a report that contains no obligation. The majority hold that it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated). Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "The correct view in my opinion regarding this verse is that the core of the meaning is the lam in His words ﴿for man﴾. When you establish what it is that a person may rightly say belongs to him, you will find it is only his striving. Whatever is added after that, such as mercy through intercession, the care of a righteous father or righteous son, the multiplication of good deeds, or Allah's deliberate bestowal of grace and mercy beyond all this, is not 'for man,' and he cannot rightly say 'this is mine' about it, except by a figurative extension and by attaching it to what is literally his." This verse was used as evidence by those who hold that no one acts on behalf of another after his death, whether with the body or with wealth; but some scholars distinguished between the body and wealth. End of quotation.

"Striving" (saʿy) means earning. "Will be seen" (yurā) is passive: i.e., he will see it present on the Day of Resurrection. The display of deeds is an honour for the doer of good and a rebuke to the wrongdoer. The pronoun in ﴿yujzāhu﴾ (he will be recompensed) refers to man, and the object pronoun refers to striving; "recompense" (al-jazāʾ) is a verbal noun. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the recompense, and then He explained it with His saying ﴿the fullest recompense﴾." If it is an explanation of the accusative verbal noun in yujzāhu, then on what is it in the accusative? And if it is an appositive, then it is of the type of substitution of a noun for a pronoun that the noun explains, a matter of disagreement, and the correct view is that it is not permitted. Al-Jumhur read ﴿and that to your Lord﴾ and what follows it from ﴿and that He﴾ with an opening hamza (anna), coordinated with what precedes it. Abu al-Sammal read them with a kasra throughout, and in His saying ﴿the fullest﴾. The threat is to the disbeliever and the promise to the believer. The "final end" (muntaha) of a thing is its ultimate point and what it reaches, i.e., the reckoning of your Lord and the gathering for its sake, as He said: ﴿and to Allah is the final return﴾, i.e., to His recompense and His reckoning, or to His reward of Paradise and His punishment of Hellfire. This explanation fits what precedes it in the verse. It is narrated from Ubayy, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and that to your Lord is the final end﴾: "Do not reflect upon the Lord." And Anas narrated from him (ﷺ): "When the Lord is mentioned, then desist."

﴿and that it is He who makes [people] laugh and weep﴾: The apparent meaning is the literal reality of laughing and weeping. Mujahid said: He made the people of Paradise laugh and the people of Hellfire weep. It has been said: laughter is a metaphor for joy, and weeping for sorrow. It has been said: He made the earth laugh with vegetation and the sky weep with rain. It has been said: He gives life through faith and causes weeping through disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿makes laugh and weeps﴾ means: He created the two faculties of laughing and weeping." End of quotation. In this there is a hint of Mu'tazilism (i'tizal, the Mu'tazili doctrine), since the actions of servants, such as laughing, weeping and others, are in their view created by the servant and not by Allah the Exalted; therefore he said: "He created the two faculties of laughing and weeping."

﴿and that He created the two mates﴾ who are paired, male and female, or other animals: ﴿from a drop of semen when it is emitted﴾: i.e., when it is poured forth, and this is the seminal fluid. It is said: "al-rajul amná and manná" (the man emitted semen). Al-Akhfash said: "when it is emitted" means: it is created and measured from the emission of the one who emits, i.e., the Measurer measured.

﴿and that upon Him is the second creation﴾: i.e., the re-creation of bodies, that is, the gathering after decay. The word "upon Him" (ʿalayhi) indicates necessity, because the existence of the thing is certain. Since the disbelievers deny this second creation, the emphasis was made by saying "upon Him," meaning its existence is inevitable, as if He, may He be exalted, made it obligatory upon Himself. The disagreement in the reading of "al-nashʾa" was mentioned in Surah al-ʿAnkabut. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He said ʿalayhi (upon Him) because it is obligatory upon Him by wisdom, so that He may recompense for good and evil." End of quotation. This is in the manner of Mu'tazilism.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 53, verses 33–62 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And that He is the One who enriches and provides (aqna)﴾: That is, He causes [people] to acquire property. It is said: qanaytu al-mal (I acquired the wealth), and aqnaytuhu iyyahu (I caused him to acquire it), meaning I caused him to acquire it. The object of aghna and aqna is not mentioned because the intent is to attribute these two actions to Allah, exalted is He. The exegetes (mufassirun) have discussed this and said there are twelve opinions, such as their saying: "He enriched Himself and made His creation poor in need of Him." Since none of these opinions has evidence to specify it, they should be taken as examples. The Sirius star (al-Shi'ra) that was worshipped is al-ʿUbur. Al-Suddi said: Himyar and Khuza'a used to worship it. Others said: The first to worship it was Abu Kabsha, one of the forefathers of the Prophet (ﷺ) on his mothers' side, and his name was ʿAbd al-Shi'ra. For this reason, the polytheists of Quraysh would call him (ﷺ) "the son of Abi Kabsha." From this is the saying of Abu Sufyan: "Indeed, the affair of the son of Abi Kabsha has become prominent." Among the Arabs there were those who revered it without worshipping it, believing in its influence on the world, and that it is one of the speaking stars. The astrologers claim this and speak of unseen matters at its rising. It crosses the sky lengthwise, while the stars cross it widthwise. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: It is Mirzam al-Jawza' (Orion's belt).

﴿And that He destroyed the first ʿAd﴾: The word huwa (He) came between "anna" (that) and its predicate, and this occurs in His saying: ﴿And that He is the One who makes laugh﴾, ﴿And that He is the One who causes death﴾, ﴿And that He is the One who enriches﴾, ﴿And that He is the Lord of Sirius﴾. As for the first three, since some people may claim this, like Nimrod's saying: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾ [al-Baqara: 258], emphasis was needed that this belongs to Allah alone and not to anyone else. He is the One who makes laugh and makes weep, He is the One who causes death and gives life, and He is the true enricher and provider. If anyone claims this, there is no reality to it. As for ﴿And that He is the Lord of Sirius﴾, since it was worshipped besides Allah, exalted is He, the text states that He, exalted is He, is its Lord and Originator. Since the creation of the pair, the other creation (al-insha' al-akhar), and the destruction of ʿAd and those mentioned, no one can claim these, so there was no need for emphasis or explicit statement that He, exalted is He, is the doer of these. The first ʿAd are the people of Hud, and the other ʿAd is Iram. It is said: The "first" refers to the ancients, because they were the first nation to be destroyed after the people of Noah, peace be upon him. It is said: The "first" refers to the eminent ones who preceded in the world; this was stated by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Zayd and the majority said: It is because they are at the beginning and ancient of time, so they are more appropriately described as "first" compared to later nations. Al-Tabari said: They were described as "the first" because the later ʿAd was a tribe that was in Mecca along with the Amalekites, and they were the Banu Luqaym ibn Hizal. Al-Mubarrad said: The later ʿAd is Thamud, and the evidence for this is the saying of Zuhayr:

*Like the red [she-camel] of ʿAd, then she is suckled and weaned*

Al-Zahrawi mentioned this. It is also said: the later ʿAd are the tyrants. It is also said: [they came] before the first, because they were before Thamud. It is also said: Thamud came before ʿAd. It is also said: the first ʿAd is ʿAd ibn Iram ibn ʿAws ibn Sam ibn Noah, and the second ʿAd are descendants of the first ʿAd.
